### LXIII.

## THE LO-CH'A COUNTRY AND THE SEA-MARKET <note>original: "Lo-ch'a Hai-shih." Lo-ch'a refers to the Rakshasas, a race of ugly, flesh-eating demons in Buddhist mythology. The "sea-market" refers to a mirage or a legendary marketplace beneath the waves.</note>

ONCE upon a time there was a young man, named Ma Chün, who was also known as Lung-mei <note>Ma is a common surname meaning "Horse"; Lung-mei translates to "Dragon-eyebrow."</note>. He was the son of a trader, and a youth of surpassing beauty. His manners were courteous, and he loved nothing better than singing and playing. He used to associate with actors, and with an embroidered handkerchief round his head the effect was that of a beautiful woman. Hence he acquired the <term>sobriquet</term> <note>A nickname or descriptive name.</note> of the Beauty. At fourteen years of age he graduated <note>This refers to passing the first level of the Imperial Civil Service examinations, a significant achievement for a young man.</note> and began to make a name for himself; but his father, who was growing old and wished to retire from business, said to him, “ My boy, book-

learning will never fill your belly or put a coat on your back; you had much better stick to the old thing." Accordingly, Ma from that time occupied himself with **scales and weights**, with **principle and interest**, and such matters <note>The "old thing" refers to the family's merchant trade. "Scales and weights" were the essential tools of a trader for weighing silver and goods, while "principle and interest" refers to the financial management of a business.</note>.

He made a voyage across the sea, and was carried away by a **typhoon** <note>original: "tai fung" or "great wind." In the 17th century, these storms were a constant peril for Chinese merchant vessels.</note>. After being tossed about for many days and nights he arrived at a country where the people were hideously ugly. When these people saw Ma they thought he was a devil and all ran screeching away. Ma was somewhat alarmed at this, but finding that it was they who were frightened at him, he quickly turned their fear to his own advantage. If he came across people eating and drinking he would rush upon them, and when they fled away for fear, he would regale himself upon what they had left.

By-and-by he went to a village among the hills, and there the people had at any rate some facial resemblance to ordinary men. But they were all in rags and tatters like beggars. So Ma sat down to rest under a tree, and the villagers, not daring to come near him, contented themselves with looking at him from a distance. They soon found, however, that he did not want to eat them, and by degrees approached a little closer to him. Ma, smiling, began to talk; and although their language was different, yet he was able to make himself tolerably intelligible, and told them whence he had come. The villagers were much pleased, and spread the news that the stranger was not a **man-eater**. Nevertheless, the very ugliest of all would only take a look and be off again; they would

...ligible to them. However, they did not come near him. Those who did go up to him were not very much unlike his own countrymen, the Chinese. They brought him plenty of food and wine. Ma asked them what they were afraid of. They replied, “We had heard from our forefathers that 26,000 *li* <term>li: A traditional Chinese unit of distance, roughly equivalent to one-third of a mile or 500 meters.</term> to the west there is a country called China. We had heard that the people of that land were the most extraordinary in appearance you can possibly imagine. Hitherto it has been hearsay; we can now believe it.” 

He then asked them how it was they were so poor. They answered, “You see, in our country everything depends, not on literary talent, but on beauty. The most beautiful are made **ministers of state**; the next handsomest are made **judges and magistrates**; and the third class in looks are employed in the palace of the king. Thus these are enabled out of their pay to provide for their wives and families. But we, from our very birth, are regarded by our parents as inauspicious, and are left to perish, some of us being occasionally preserved by more humane parents to prevent the extinction of the family.” 

Ma asked the name of their country, and they told him it was **Lo-ch‘a** <note>original: "Lo-ch‘a." This is the Chinese transliteration of "Rakshasa," a type of man-eating demon in Hindu and Buddhist mythology. In this satirical story, the "demons" consider the handsome Ma to be the monster.</note>. Also that the capital city was some 30 *li* to the north. He begged them to take him there, and next day at cock-crow he started thitherwards in their company, arriving just about dawn. The walls of the city were made of black stone, as black as ink, and the city gate-houses were about 100 feet high. Red stones were used for tiles, and picking up a broken piece Ma found that it marked his finger-nail like **vermilion** <note>A brilliant red pigment made from cinnabar, traditionally used in China for official seals and high-quality ink.</note>. They arrived just when the Court was rising, and saw all the

...carriages and processions of the high officials. The villagers pointed out one individual whom they identified as the **Prime Minister** <term>Prime Minister: In the original text, the *Zaixiang*, the highest-ranking civil official who advised the Emperor.</term>. His ears hung forward in large flaps; he possessed three nostrils, and his eyelashes were long and thick, resembling bamboo screens hanging in front of his eyes. Following him, several others emerged on horseback; the villagers identified these as the **privy councillors** <note>High-ranking advisors to the monarch.</note>. They continued to point out the various ranks of all the grotesque and strange-looking men they saw. Ma noticed a pattern: the lower an official's rank, the less hideous they appeared to be.

Eventually, Ma began his return journey. The people in the streets were filled with great wonder at the sight of him, stumbling over one another in a frantic rush as if they had encountered a **goblin** <note>Because Ma is "normal-looking" to us, he is considered a terrifying monster in this land where beauty and ugliness are inverted.</note>. The villagers accompanying him shouted out to reassure the crowds, who then stood at a safe distance just to stare. 

By the time he returned to the village, there was not a man, woman, or child in the entire nation who did not know that a "strange man" was staying there. The gentry and the officials became very curious to see him. However, whenever Ma approached any of their houses, the gatekeepers would slam the doors in his face. The masters, their wives, and their families would only dare to peek at him and speak to him through the cracks in the doors. 

Not a single person dared to meet him face-to-face. Finally, the villagers, at a loss for what to do, thought of a man who had been sent by a previous king on official business to foreign nations. "Since he has seen many different types of men," they said, "he will not be afraid of you." They went to his house, where they were received in a very friendly manner. This man appeared to be about eighty or ninety years old; his eyeballs protruded from his head, and his beard curled outward, as coarse as the quills of a hedgehog. He said,

“In my youth I was sent by the king among many nations, but I never went to China <note>original: "Zhongzhou," referring to the central lands of China.</note>. I am now one hundred and twenty years of age, and that I should be permitted to see a native of your country is a fact which it will be my duty to report to the **Throne** <note>The seat of power for the King of the Rakshasas.</note>. For ten years and more I have not been to **Court**, but have remained here in seclusion ; yet I will now make an effort on your behalf.” 

Then followed a banquet, and when the wine had already circulated pretty freely, some dozen singing girls came in and sang and danced before them. The girls all wore white embroidered turbans, and long scarlet robes which trailed on the ground. The words they uttered were unintelligible, and the tunes they played perfectly hideous <note>In this land, aesthetic values are inverted: what Ma finds screeching and discordant, the locals find beautiful.</note>. 

The host, however, seemed to enjoy it very much, and said to Ma “Have you music in China?” He replied that they had, and the old man asked for a specimen. Ma hummed him a tune, beating time on the table, with which he was very much pleased, declaring that his guest had the ‘**voice of a phœnix and the notes of a dragon**,’ <note>A traditional idiom denoting music of divine or extraordinary beauty.</note> such as he had never heard before. 

The next day he presented a **memorial** <term>Memorial: A formal written statement or petition addressed to a sovereign (in Chinese, *zou-zhe*).</term> to the Throne, and the king at once commanded Ma to appear before him. Several of the ministers, however, represented that his appearance was so **hideous** <note>To the Rakshasas, Ma’s "normal" human face is considered a grotesque deformity.</note> it might frighten His Majesty, and the king accordingly desisted from his intention. The old man returned and told Ma, being quite upset about it. They remained together some time until they had drunk themselves tipsy. Then Ma, seizing a sword, began to **attitudinize** <note>To strike dramatic, stylized poses, likely mimicking the movements of traditional Chinese theater.</note>, smearing his face all over with coal-dust. He acted the part of **Chang** <note>Refers to Zhang Fei, a legendary general from the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*. In opera, Zhang Fei is portrayed with a fierce, jet-black painted face.</note>

<summary>Ma meets an elderly official who tries to introduce him to the King, but Ma's "normal" appearance is deemed too ugly for a royal audience. To cope with the rejection, Ma disguises himself with black face paint in the style of a fierce opera character.</summary>

**Zhang Fei** <note>original: "Chang Fei." A legendary general from the **Three Kingdoms** period (220–280 AD) known for his dark skin and fierce, bristling appearance. In Chinese opera, his face is painted coal-black.</note>, at which his host was so delighted that he begged him to appear before the **Prime Minister** in the character of **Zhang Fei**. Ma replied, "I don't mind a little amateur acting, but how can I play the hypocrite <note>The author uses this moment to satirize how people in the real world must often wear "masks" or disguise their true nature to achieve success.</note> for my own personal advantage?" On being pressed, he consented, and the old man prepared a great feast and asked some of the high officials to be present, telling Ma to paint himself as before. 

When the guests had arrived, Ma was brought out to see them; whereupon they all exclaimed, "**Oh, my!** <note>original: "Ai-yah!"—a common Chinese exclamation of surprise or shock.</note> How is it he was so ugly before and is now so beautiful?" By-and-by, when they were all taking wine together, Ma began to sing them a most bewitching song, and they got so excited over it that the next day they recommended him to the king. 

The king sent a special summons for him to appear and asked him many questions about the government of China, to all of which Ma replied in detail, eliciting sighs of admiration from His Majesty. He was honoured with a banquet in the royal guest-pavilion, and when the king had made himself tipsy, he said to him, "I hear you are a very skilful musician. Will you be good enough to let me hear you?" Ma then got up and began to perform theatrical gestures, singing a plaintive air like the **girls with the turbans** <note>Referring to the local Rakshasa dancers mentioned on the previous page, whose music Ma originally found hideous.</note>. The king was charmed and at once made him a **privy councillor** <term>Privy Councillor: A high-ranking advisor to a monarch; here, it refers to a position close to the King's personal circle.</term>, giving him a private banquet and bestowing other marks of royal favour. ...[they were] going to start, so that he might accompany them; but they begged him not to think of doing so. He replied, “I am a sailor: how can I be afraid of wind and waves?” Very soon after this, people arrived with merchandise to be transported, and so Ma packed his bags and went on board the vessel that was departing.

This vessel held several dozen people and was flat-bottomed with a railing all the way around. Rowed by ten men, it cut through the water as swiftly as an arrow. After a voyage of three days, they saw in the distance the faint outlines of towers and **minarets** <note>The original English translator used this term to describe the tall, slender towers of the undersea city, evoking an exotic, palace-like atmosphere.</note>, and crowds of trading vessels. They soon arrived at the city. The walls were constructed of bricks as long as a man’s body, and the tops of its buildings were lost in the **Milky Way** <note>original: 天河 (tiānhé). Literally the "Silver River." In Chinese cosmology, the celestial river of stars and the earthly oceans were sometimes thought to be connected.</note>.⁶ Having secured their boat, they went inside and saw rare pearls and wondrous precious stones of dazzling beauty laid out in the market—treasures quite unknown among the world of men. 

Then, they saw a young man come forth riding upon a beautiful steed. The people in the market moved back to let him pass, saying he was the third son of the King. However, when the Prince saw Ma, he exclaimed, “This is no foreigner!” <note>In the previous land Ma visited, his natural human face was considered a hideous "foreign" deformity. Ma bowed and, standing to one side, told them his name and family history. The Prince smiled and said, “For you to have honored our country with a visit is a great piece of good luck.” He then gave Ma a horse and invited him to follow. The horses plunged into the water. Ma was terribly frightened and screamed out; but the sea opened dry before them and formed a wall of water on either side <note>This imagery of the sea parting is a common motif in Chinese folklore to indicate that a mortal has entered a divine or watery realm.</note>. In a little time they reached the king's palace, the beams of which were made of tortoise-shell and the tiles of fishes' scales. The four walls were of crystal, and dazzled the eye like mirrors. They got down off their horses and went in, and Ma was introduced to the king.

The young prince said, "Sire, I have been to the market, and have got a gentleman from China." Whereupon Ma made obeisance before the king, who addressed him as follows:—"Sir, from a talented scholar like yourself I venture to ask for a few stanzas upon our sea-market. Pray do not refuse." Ma thereupon made a *kot'ow* <note>original: 叩頭 (kòutóu). A deep bow performed by kneeling and touching one's head to the ground as a sign of respect to a superior.</note>, and undertook the king's command. Using an ink-slab of crystal, a brush of **dragon's beard** <note>original: 龍鬚 (lóngxū). While literally "dragon's beard," this likely refers to a high-quality calligraphy brush made from fine, stiff animal hair.</note>, paper as white as snow, and ink scented like the larkspur,⁷ Ma immediately threw off some thousand odd verses, which he laid at the feet of the king.

The lookers-on were much alarmed, but in a moment there was a flash of lightning, followed by a clap of thunder and a squall of rain, and she was gone.

### LXIV.

## THE FIGHTING CRICKET.

DURING the reign of <term>Hsüan Tê</term> <note>original: "Hsüan Tê" — The Xuande Emperor (reigned 1425–1435) of the Ming dynasty. While historically seen as a period of stability, folk tradition remembers him as the "Cricket Emperor" due to his obsession with the sport.</note>, <term>cricket fighting</term> <note>A traditional Chinese pastime where two male crickets are placed in a bowl to fight. During the Ming era, it evolved from a simple folk game into an expensive and high-stakes imperial craze.</note> was very much in vogue at court, levies of crickets being exacted from the people as a tax. On one occasion the magistrate of <term>Hua-yin</term> <note>A district in Shaanxi Province, famous for being the gateway to the sacred Mount Hua.</note>, wishing to make friends with the Governor, presented him with a cricket which, on being set to fight, displayed very remarkable powers; so much so that the Governor commanded the magistrate to supply him regularly with these insects. The latter, in his turn, ordered the <term>beadles</term> <note>original: "beadles" — These were local headmen or neighborhood monitors (known as *Lizheng*) chosen from reputable families. They were held personally responsible for the collection of taxes and the conduct of their neighbors.</note> of his district to provide him with crickets; and then it became a practice for people who had nothing else to do to catch and rear them for this purpose. Thus the price of crickets rose very high; and when the beadle’s <margin>These local officials often faced financial ruin if they could not satisfy the demands of their superiors, as they were forced to make up any deficit from their own pockets.</margin> runners came to

Now in the village of which we are speaking there lived a man named **Ch'êng**, a student who had often failed for his bachelor's degree; and, being a stupid sort of fellow, his name was sent in for the post of <term>beadle</term> <note>original: "beadle" — Referring to the *Lizheng*, a local village headman. Unlike a volunteer position, this was a mandatory and often ruinous administrative burden placed on middle-class families to ensure tax collection.</note>. He did all he could to get out of it, but without success; and by the end of the year his small patrimony was gone. Just then came a call for crickets, and **Ch'êng**, not daring to make a like call upon his neighbours, was at his wits' end, and in his distress determined to commit suicide. "What's the use of that?" cried his wife. "You'd do better to go out and try to find some." So off went **Ch'êng** in the early morning, with a bamboo tube and a silk net, not returning till late at night; and he searched about in tumble-down walls, in bushes, under stones, and in holes, but without catching more than two or three, do what he would. Even those he did catch were weak creatures, and of no use at all, which made the magistrate fix a limit of time, the result of which was that in a few days **Ch'êng** got one hundred blows with the <term>bamboo</term> <note>A standard form of corporal punishment where the recipient was beaten with a heavy wooden lath. It was intended to "motivate" officials to fulfill their quotas.</note>. This made him so sore that he was quite unable to go after the crickets any more, and,

### LXV.

## TAKING REVENGE.

**Hsiang Kao**, otherwise called **Ch’u-tan**, was a man from **Taiyuan** <note>A major historical city in northern China, the capital of Shanxi province.</note> who was deeply attached to his half-brother **Shêng**. **Shêng** himself was desperately enamoured of a young lady named **Po-ssŭ** <note>original: "Po-ssŭ" (波斯). This is the Chinese term for **Persia**. At the time, this name was often used as a metaphor for "valuables" or "jewels" because of the exotic goods imported from that region. To be "poor in Persia" was a common idiom for having few jewels or gold ornaments.</note>, who was also very fond of him; however, the girl’s mother wanted too much money for her daughter’s hand in marriage.

Now, a rich young fellow named **Chuang** thought he should like to get **Po-ssŭ** for himself, and proposed to buy her as a **concubine** <term>A secondary wife with lower legal and social status than a primary wife, often purchased or taken from a lower social class.</term>. 

"No, no," said **Po-ssŭ** to her mother, "I prefer being **Shêng’s** wife to becoming **Chuang’s** concubine." 

So her mother consented and informed **Shêng**, who had only recently buried his first wife; at which he was delighted and made preparations to take her over to his own house. When **Chuang** heard this, he was infuriated against **Shêng** for thus depriving him of **Po-ssŭ**; and chancing to meet him out one day, he set to and abused him—

->### LXVI.<-

->## THE TIPSY TURTLE.<-

At **Lin-t‘iao** <note>Modern-day Min County in Gansu Province, China.</note> there lived a **Mr. Fêng** <note>Original: "Feng." A common Chinese surname.</note>, whose other name the person who told me this story could not remember; he belonged to a good family, though now somewhat falling into decay. Now a certain man, who caught turtles, owed him some money which he could not pay, but whenever he captured any turtles he used to send one to Mr. Fêng. One day he took him an enormous creature, with a white spot on its forehead; but Fêng was so struck with something in its appearance, that he let it go again. A little afterwards he was returning home from his son-in-law’s, and had reached the banks of the river,¹ when in the dusk of the evening he saw a drunken man come rolling along, attended by two or three servants.

---

¹ The name here used is the **Hêng** <note>Original: "Heng" (恒), meaning constant or ceaseless.</note> or “ceaseless” river, which is applied by the Chinese to the **Ganges** <note>The sacred river of India, often used in Buddhist literature as a metaphor for the infinite.</note>. A certain number, extending to fifty-three places of figures, is called “Ganges sand,” in allusion to a famous remark that “**Buddha** <term>The "Enlightened One," founder of Buddhism.</term> and the **Bôdhisatvas** <term>Beings who have attained enlightenment but remain in the world to help others.</term> knew of the creation and destruction of every grain of dust in **Jambudwipa** <term>In ancient Indian and Buddhist cosmology, this refers to the world inhabited by ordinary humans.</term> (the universe); how much more the number of the sand-particles in the river Ganges?”

## LXVII.

# THE MAGIC PATH.

IN the province of Guangdong <note>original: "Kuangtung"</note> there lived a scholar named Guo <note>original: "Kuo"</note>, who was one evening on his way home from a friend’s, when he lost his way among the hills. He got into a thick jungle, where, after about an hour’s wandering, he suddenly heard the sound of laughing and talking on the top of the hill. Hurrying up in the direction of the sound, he beheld some ten or a dozen persons sitting on the ground engaged in drinking. No sooner had they caught sight of Guo than they all cried out, “Come along! just room for one more; you’re in the nick of time.” So Guo sat down with the company, most of whom, he noticed, belonged to the *literati* <note>original: "literati." This term refers to the "scholar-official" class in imperial China. While it includes all literary men of any rank, it is often used for those who have passed the lower civil service exams but have not yet secured an official government post. Many supported themselves by tutoring or continued studying for higher degrees.</note>,¹ and began by asking them to direct him on his way home;

---

<note>¹ This term, while really including all literary men, of no matter what rank or standing, is more usually confined to that large section of unemployed scholarship made up of (1) those who are waiting to get started in an official career, (2) those who have taken one or more degrees and are preparing for the next, (3) those who have failed to distinguish themselves at the public examinations <note>The Imperial Examination system was the primary route to social status and political power in China, testing candidates on Confucian classics.</note>, and eke out a small patrimony by taking pupils, and (4) scholars of sufficiently high qualifications who have no taste for official life.</note>

After a while, he imitated a parrot and cried out, “Mr. Guo is very drunk; you had better see him home!” Then the sounds ceased, only to begin again a moment later. ## LXVIII.

### THE FAITHLESS WIDOW. <note>In traditional Chinese society, it was considered highly disreputable for a widow to remarry, as she was expected to remain loyal to her deceased husband's family and care for his children and elders.</note>

MR. NIU was a Kiangsi <note>Modern-day Jiangxi province in southeast China.</note> man who traded in piece goods <term>piece goods</term> <note>Textile fabrics produced in standard lengths, such as silk, cotton, or linen, which were major commodities in trade.</note>. He married a wife from the Chêng family, by whom he had two children, a boy and a girl. When thirty-three years of age he fell ill and died, his son Chung being then only twelve and his little girl eight or nine.

His wife did not remain faithful to his memory, but, selling off all the property, pocketed the proceeds and married another man, leaving her two children almost in a state of destitution with their aunt, Niu’s sister-in-law, an old lady of sixty, who had lived with them previously, and had now nowhere to seek a shelter. <note>The aunt's situation highlights the vulnerability of the elderly in this period when the primary family structure collapsed.</note>

---

<note>Unless under exceptional circumstances, it is not considered creditable in China for widows to marry again. It may here be mentioned that the honorary tablets <term>honorary tablets</term> <note>Also known as "Pailou" or "Biaozhang," these were commemorative plaques or arches granted by the Emperor to recognize individuals for extreme filial piety or lifelong chastity.</note> conferred from time to time by His Imperial Majesty upon virtuous widows are only given to women who, widowed before the age of thirty, have remained in that state for a period of thirty years. The meaning of this is obvious: temptations are supposed to be fewer and less dangerous after thirty, which is the equivalent of forty with us; and it is wholly improbable that thirty years of virtuous life, at which period the widow would be at least fifty, would be followed by any act that might cast a stain upon the tablet thus bestowed.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the story of a merchant's widow who, breaking social custom, sells her deceased husband's property to remarry, abandoning her young children and elderly sister-in-law. It also provides historical context on the "virtuous widow" honors granted in imperial China.</summary>

## THE PRINCESS LILY.

In the district of <term>Chiao-chou</term><note>Modern Jiaozhou, a city in Shandong Province, China.</note>, there lived a man named <term>Tou Hsün</term><note>Pinyin: Dou Xun.</note>, who also went by the name Hsiao-hui. One day, just as he had drifted off to sleep, he saw a man dressed in <term>serge</term><note>A sturdy, twilled woolen cloth, typically worn by servants or commoners in this era.</note> standing beside his bed. The man seemed very eager to tell him something. 

Tou asked what he wanted, and the man replied that he had been sent to deliver an invitation from his master. 

"And who is your master?" Tou asked. 

"Oh, he lives quite close by," the man answered. 

So the two of them set off together. After walking for a while, they arrived at a place filled with countless white houses, built one above the other and shaded by thick groves of lemon trees. ### LXXIII.

## THE UNJUST SENTENCE.

MR. CHU was a native of Yang-ku <note>Now Yanggu County in Shandong Province, China.</note>, and, as a young man, was much given to playing tricks and talking in a loose kind of way. Having lost his wife, he went off to ask a certain old woman to arrange another match <note>In this period, professional matchmakers were essential for navigating the complex social and legal requirements of marriage.</note> for him; and on the way, he chanced to fall in with a neighbour’s wife who took his fancy very much. So he said in joke to the old woman, “Get me that stylish-looking, handsome lady, and I shall be quite satisfied.” “I’ll see what I can do,” replied the old woman, also joking, “if you will manage to kill her present husband;” upon which Chu laughed and said he certainly would do so.

In imperial China, this involved detailed forensic examinations by officials to determine the cause of death.</note></term>, but was unable to find any clue to the murderer. ### LXXV.

## THE THREE STATES OF EXISTENCE.

A CERTAIN man of the province of **Hunan** could recall what had happened to him in three previous lives. In the first, he was a **magistrate**; and, on one occasion, when he had been nominated <term>Assistant-Examiner — A temporary official post within the Imperial Examination system, responsible for the first round of grading candidate essays before passing them to a superior.</term> <note>original: "Assistant-Examiner," referring to the civil service examinations of Imperial China. The **Examiner** was immediately summoned to take his trial, and when he arrived the **King** asked him, saying, “As you are appointed to examine the various essays, how is it that you throw out the able and admit the worthless?” 

“Sire,” replied he, “the ultimate decision rests with the **Grand Examiner**; I only pass them on to him.”

On one occasion, he happened to pass through the prefectural city just as the examination for **bachelor's degree** <note>The *Xiucai* degree, the entry-level qualification for the scholar-gentry class.</note> was over; and the candidate who had come out at the top of the list, though named **Li**, was no other than **Mr. Hsing**. So he led this man away, and took him to an inn, where he treated him with the utmost cordiality, finally arranging that, as **Mr. Li** was still unmarried, he should marry his pretty daughter. 

Everyone, of course, thought that this was done in admiration of **Li's** talents, ignorant that destiny had already decreed the union of the young couple. No sooner were they married than **Li**, proud of his own literary achievements, began to slight his father-in-law, and often passed many months without going near him; all of which the father-in-law bore very patiently. When, at length, **Li** had repeatedly failed to get on any farther in his career, the father-in-law even went so far as to set to work, by all manner of means, to secure his success; after which they lived happily together as father and son.

**HSI FANG-P'ING** <note>Pinyin: Xi Fangping.</note> was a native of **Tung-an** <note>Modern-day Dongan.</note>. His father's name was **Hsi-Lien**—a hasty-tempered man, who had quarrelled with a neighbour named **Yang**. He was much **chagrined** <note>original: *chagrined*, meaning feeling distressed or humiliated by a failure or disappointment.</note> at this, and wished to go back as fast as he could; he, therefore, dismissed his servant, and on shutting his eyes once more, he found everything just as he had left it, except that where, on the first occasion, he had observed the young girls, there were none now to be seen, but only some dishevelled hump-backed creatures, who cried out at him, and asked him what he meant by spying about there. **Ku** didn’t dare reply, but hurried past them as quickly as he could, and on to the **pavilion** of the young Prince. There he found him still sitting, but with a black beard over a foot in length; and the Prince was anxious to know where he had been, saying that seven scenes of the play were already over. He then seized a big **goblet** of wine, and made **Ku** drink it as a penalty, by which time the play was finished, and the list was handed up for a further selection. The “**Marriage of P'êng Tsu**” <note>original: *P'êng Tsu*, a legendary figure in Chinese mythology often called the "Chinese Methuselah," said to have lived over 800 years. The play likely deals with themes of longevity.</note> was selected, and then the singing-girls began to hand round the wine in **cocoa-nuts** big enough to hold about five quarts, which **Ku** declined, on the ground that he was suffering from weak eyes, and was consequently afraid to drink too much. “If your eyes are bad,” cried the young Prince, “the **Court physician** <term>**Court physician**: a high-ranking doctor appointed to treat members of the imperial or royal family.</term> is at hand,”

### LXXVIII.

## CHOU K’O-CH’ANG AND HIS GHOST.

In the region of Huai-shang <note>Huai-shang refers to the area "on the Huai River" in eastern China.</note> there lived a scholar named **Chou T'ien-i** <note>original: "graduate" — specifically a *xiucai*, a person who has passed the entry-level civil service examinations in the Imperial system.</note>. Although he was fifty years old, he had only one son, called **K'o-ch'ang**, whom he loved very dearly. This boy, when he was about thirteen or fourteen, was a handsome and healthy-looking fellow, but he was strangely resistant to his studies. He often played truant from school, sometimes for the entire day, without any scolding or discipline from his father. 

One day he went away and did not come back in the evening; even after a thorough search, no traces of him could be discovered. His father and mother were in despair and hardly cared to live anymore. But after more than a year had passed, lo and behold! **K'o-ch'ang** returned. He said that he had been lured away by a **Taoist priest** <note>In Chinese folklore, Taoist priests are often portrayed as wandering figures with supernatural powers, capable of both helping and abducting people for various spiritual reasons.</note> who, however, had not done him any harm. He explained that he had seized a moment while the priest was absent to escape and find his way home again. 

His father was delighted and asked him no more questions, but immediately set to work to give him an education. **K'o-ch'ang** turned out to be much cleverer and more intelligent than he had been before, so much so that by the following year he had already taken his

### LXXIX.

## THE SPIRITS OF PO-YANG LAKE.

An official named **Chai** was appointed to a post at **Jao-chou** <note>A historical region in what is now Jiangxi Province, China.</note>, and on his way there, he crossed the **Po-yang lake** <note>China's largest freshwater lake, famous for its beauty and its sudden, dangerous storms.</note>. Happening to visit a shrine dedicated to the local spirits, he noticed a carved image of the patriotic **Ting P'u-lang** <note>original: "丁普郎" — A historical figure and general who served under the first Ming Emperor; he was known for a legendary death in battle where he continued to stand upright even after being decapitated.</note>, and another statue of a spirit who shared his own surname, **Chai**. This second statue was placed in a very inferior, lowly position within the shrine.

"Come, come!" said **Chai**, "My namesake saint should not be put in the background like that." 

He personally moved the image into a more honorable place and then returned to his boat. Soon after, a great wind struck the vessel, carrying away the mast and the sails. The sailors, in a state of great alarm, began to howl and cry in fear for their lives. However, in just a few moments, they saw a small skiff come cutting through the waves toward them. Before long, they were all safely brought on board the smaller boat. 

The man who rowed the skiff looked strangely like the statue in the shrine—the very one whose position **Chai** had changed. But they were hardly out of danger when the squall passed over, and both the skiff and the man vanished into thin air.

<summary>An official shows respect to a neglected statue of a namesake spirit in a lakeside shrine. In gratitude, the spirit appears in human form to rescue the official and his crew from a sudden, life-threatening shipwreck.</summary>

<keywords>Po-yang Lake, Ting P'u-lang, Official Chai, Ming Dynasty, spirit intervention, Chinese folklore, Jao-chou, divine gratitude</keywords>

### LXXX.

## THE STREAM OF CASH.

A certain gentleman’s servant was one day in his master’s garden, when he beheld a **stream of cash** <term>cash: the primary currency of imperial China, these were small, circular copper or bronze coins with a square hole in the middle, often carried on strings</term> flowing by, two or three feet in breadth and of about the same depth. He immediately seized two large handfuls, and then threw himself down on the top of the stream in order to try and secure the rest. However, when he got up he found that it had all flowed away from under him, none being left except what he had got in his two hands.

->[ “Ah!” says the commentator, “money is properly a **circulating medium** <note>The commentator is making a play on words: money is meant to "circulate" or flow like water through society, not to be dammed up or hoarded by one person.</note>, and is not intended for a man to lie upon and keep all to himself.” ]<-

---

<margin>See Story No. II, note 2, regarding the history of Chinese coinage.</margin>

<note>The Chinese, fond as they are of introducing water—often in the form of miniature lakes—into their gardens and pleasure-grounds, do not always approve of a running stream near a dwelling-house. The translator notes a case of a man who lived in a rent-free house next to a mountain-rill; despite the beauty of the location, he moved out and paid for his own lodgings because he believed the stream *carried all his good luck away*. This belief was held even by a **graduate** <term>graduate: a scholar who had passed the civil service examinations, the highest level of education in imperial China</term>.</note>

<summary>A servant attempts to hoard a literal river of flowing coins, only to find that wealth cannot be pinned down by force. The story serves as a metaphor for the intended "circulation" of money within a society.</summary>

### LXXXI.

## THE INJUSTICE OF HEAVEN.

MR. HSU was a **magistrate** <term>magistrate: a local government official in imperial China who acted as both administrator and judge</term> at Shantung. A certain upper chamber of his house was used as a store-room; but some creature managed so frequently to get in and make havoc among the stores, for which the servants were always being scolded, that at length some of the latter determined to keep watch. By-and-by they saw a huge spider as big as a **peck measure** <term>peck measure: a traditional dry volume unit, roughly the size of a large bucket or basket</term>, and hurried off to tell their master, who thought it so strange that he gave orders to the servants to feed the insect with cakes. It thus became very tame, and would always come forth when hungry, returning as soon as it had taken enough to eat.<sup>1</sup> Years passed away, and one day Mr. Hsü was consulting his **archives** <term>archives: official government records and legal documents</term>, when suddenly the spider appeared and ran under the table. Thinking it was hungry, he bade his servants give it a cake; but the next moment he noticed two snakes, of about the thickness of a chop-stick, lying one on each side. The spider

### 82. <note>original: "LXXXII."</note>

## THE SEA-SERPENT.

A merchant <term>Chia: A common surname in these tales, sometimes used by the author Pu Songling as a pun on the word for "falsehood," though here it likely identifies a specific trader.</term> was traveling on the southern seas <note>likely referring to the South China Sea, a major trade route during the Qing Dynasty.</note>, when one night the ship was suddenly illuminated as if it were broad daylight. Rushing to see what was happening, he saw a massive creature with its body half-submerged, rising up like a mountain. Its eyes were like two suns, casting a brilliant light in all directions. When the merchant asked the sailors what it was, no one could identify it. They all crouched down and watched it; eventually, the monster sank back into the water, and everything returned to darkness as before. Upon arriving at the port, they found that all the local people were discussing a mysterious bright light that had appeared in the night. The timing of their sightings matched exactly with the strange scene the crew had witnessed.<sup>1</sup>

### LXXXIV.

## COURAGE TESTED.

MR. TUNG was a man from Hsü-chou <note>A city in northern Jiangsu province, historically known for its strong martial arts culture and the toughness of its people.</note> who was very fond of practicing the broad-sword. He was a light-hearted, adventurous fellow, though his impulsive nature often led him into various difficulties. One day, while traveling, he encountered a stranger riding a mule who was heading in the same direction. They struck up a conversation and eventually began to discuss various feats of physical strength and martial skill. 

The traveller explained that his name was T'ung <note>original: "T'ung" (童). The translator points out that although this name sounds similar to the protagonist's name, "Tung" (董), they are written with entirely different characters and pronounced with different tones. To a Chinese ear, they are as distinct as "Brown" and "Jones."</note> and that he hailed from Liao-yang. He mentioned that he had been away from his home for twenty years and had recently returned from a journey across the sea. 

“Then I venture to say,” cried Tung, “that in your wanderings across the Four Seas <note>The "Four Seas" is a traditional term referring to the boundaries of the habitable world. In ancient Chinese cosmology, the world was often envisioned as a square, with China—the "Middle Kingdom"—at its center, surrounded by these seas. Beyond these waters, the Chinese believed there were scattered islands inhabited by various foreign nations.</note>—”

"You have seen a great many people; but have you seen any supernaturally clever ones?" <note>original: "shen-hsien" (神仙). This refers to Daoist immortals or beings who have achieved supernatural powers through spiritual cultivation.</note> Tung asked him to what he alluded; and then Tung explained what his own particular hobby was, adding how much he would like to learn from them any tricks in the art of the broad-sword <term>broad-sword: a "dao," a single-edged Chinese sword used for slashing and chopping</term>.

It needs but that a man should be a loyal subject and a filial son <note>Filial piety—devotion to one's parents—was considered the highest virtue in Chinese society and a prerequisite for achieving any higher spiritual state.</note> for him to know all that the supernaturals know."

Tung handed it to him, and, when he had turned it over two or three times, he said, "This is a very inferior piece of steel; now, though I know nothing about broad-swords myself, I have a weapon which is really of some use." 

He then drew from beneath his coat a sword of a foot or so in length, and with it he began to pare pieces off Tung's sword, which seemed as soft as a melon, and which he cut quite away like a horse's hoof <note>This is a vivid comparison to the way a farrier trims a horse’s hoof—showing that the traveler's blade sliced through metal as if it were mere horn or organic matter.</note>. Tung was greatly astonished, and borrowed the other's sword to examine it, returning it after carefully wiping the blade. He then invited T'ung to his house, and made him stay the night; and, after begging him to explain the mystery of his sword, began to nurse his leg and sit listening respectfully without saying a word. ² These matches consist simply of thin strips of wood dipped in sulfur <note>original: "brimstone"</note>, and resemble those used in England as late as the first quarter of the present century. ### LXXXVII.

## A STRANGE COMPANION.

Han Kung-fu, of Yü-ch‘êng, <note>Yü-ch‘êng (Yucheng) is a county in the Shandong province of China, the region where many of these stories originate.</note> told me that he was one day travelling along a road with a man of his village, named P‘eng, when all of a sudden the latter disappeared, leaving his mule to jog along with an empty saddle. At the same moment, Mr. Han heard his voice calling for assistance, and apparently proceeding from inside one of the panniers <note>Panniers are large baskets or bags, typically slung in pairs across the back of a pack animal like a mule or donkey.</note> strapped across the mule’s back; and on looking closely, there indeed he was in one of the panniers, which, however, did not seem to be at all displaced by his weight. On trying to get him out the mouth of the pannier closed itself tightly; and it was only when he cut it open with a knife that he saw P‘êng curled up in it like a dog. He then helped him out, and asked him how he managed to get in; but this he was unable to say. It further appeared that his family was under fox influence, <term>fox influence: In Chinese folklore, fox spirits (huli jing) are shape-shifters known for their mischievous and sometimes malevolent supernatural powers, including the ability to shrink people or transport them into small spaces.</term> many strange things of this kind having happened before.

<summary>A man named P'eng mysteriously vanishes from his mule's saddle only to be found shrunken and trapped inside a small pack-basket. The strange event is attributed to a "fox influence" or haunting that plagued his family.</summary>

## LXXXVIII.
# SPIRITUALISTIC SÉANCES.

It is customary in Shantung <note>Now known as Shandong, a coastal province in East China where many of these tales are set.</note>, when any one is sick, for the womenfolk to engage an old sorceress or medium, who strums on a tambourine and performs certain mysterious antics. This custom obtains even more in the capital, where young ladies of the best families frequently organize such *séances* <note>A meeting where people attempt to make contact with the world of spirits.</note> among themselves. On a table in the hall they spread out a profusion of wine and meat, and burn huge candles which make the place as light as day. Then the sorceress, shortening her skirts, stands on one leg and performs the *shang-yang* <term>shang-yang: A mythical one-legged bird. In ancient lore, its appearance was said to predict heavy rain.</term>,¹ while two of the others support her, one on each side. All this time she is chattering unintelligible sentences,² some-

## LXXXIX.

### THE MYSTERIOUS HEAD.

Several traders <note>Traveling merchants were common figures in these stories, often staying in shared quarters at inns during long journeys.</note> who were lodging at an inn in Peking <note>original: "Peking," the historical name for Beijing, the capital of China.</note>, occupied a room which was divided from the adjoining apartment by a partition of boards from which a piece was missing, leaving an aperture <note>A hole or opening.</note> about as big as a basin. Suddenly a girl's head appeared through the opening, with very pretty features and nicely dressed hair; and the next moment an arm, as white as polished jade <term>Jade (yu): In Chinese literature, "mutton-fat" white jade is the standard of beauty for fair, smooth, and clear skin.</term>. The traders were much alarmed, and, thinking it was the work of devils <note>The original term likely refers to *gui* (ghosts or demons), which were believed to haunt travelers.</note>, tried to seize the head, which, however, was quickly drawn in again out of their reach. 

This happened a second time, and then, as they could see no body belonging to the head, one of them took a knife in his hand and crept up against the partition underneath the hole. In a little while the head re-appeared, when he made a chop at it and cut it off, the blood spurting out all over the floor and wall. 

The traders hurried off to tell the landlord, who immediately reported the matter to the authorities <note>Local government officials who acted as both police and judges in imperial China.</note>, taking the head with him, and the traders were forthwith arrested and

### XC.

## THE SPIRIT OF THE HILLS.

A MAN named **Li**, of **I-tu** <note>original: "I-tu," referring to modern-day Yidu in Shandong Province, China.</note>, was once crossing the hills when he came upon a number of persons sitting on the ground engaged in drinking. As soon as they saw **Li** they begged him to join them, and vied with each other in filling his cup. Meanwhile, he looked about him and noticed that the various trays and dishes contained all kinds of costly food ; the wine only seemed to him a little rough on the palate. In the middle of their fun up came a stranger with a face about three feet long and a very tall hat ; whereupon the others were very much alarmed, and cried out, "The <term>hill spirit</term> <note>In Chinese folklore, mountain spirits or "shanshen" are powerful deities or creatures that guard the wilderness; they are often depicted as strange or frightening in appearance.</note> ! the hill spirit !" running away in all directions as fast as they could go. **Li** hid himself in a hole in the ground ; and when by-and-by he peeped out to see what had happened, the wine and food had disappeared, and there was nothing there but a few dirty <term>potsherds</term> <note>Fragments of broken ceramic pottery.</note> and some pieces of broken tiles with <term>efts</term> <note>A term for small newts or salamanders.</note> and lizards crawling over them. <note>The original translator, Herbert Giles, noted that the character Li had likely drunk too much alcohol before his walk, implying the "feast" was a drunken hallucination or a trick played by mountain spirits.</note>

### XCI.

## INGRATITUDE PUNISHED.

**K'u Ta-yu** was a native of the **Yang district** <note>Likely referring to Yangzhou in Jiangsu Province.</note>, and managed to get a military appointment under the command of **Tsu Shu-shun**. <note>original: "Of whom I can learn nothing." The translator, Herbert Giles, noted that he could find no historical records for this specific individual.</note> The latter treated him most kindly, and finally sent him as **Major-General** of some troops by which he was then trying to establish the dynasty of the **usurping Chows** <note>This refers to the "Great Zhou" dynasty (1678–1681) declared by the rebel general Wu Sangui during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories against the Qing Dynasty.</note>. **K'u** soon perceived that the game was lost, and immediately turned his forces upon **Tsu Shu-shun**, whom he succeeded in capturing, after **Tsu** had been wounded in the hand, and whom he at once forwarded as a prisoner to headquarters.

That night he dreamed that the <term>Judge of Purgatory</term> <note>In Chinese folklore, this is Yanluo Wang, the sovereign of the underworld who oversees the judgment of souls and assigns punishments based on their earthly sins.</note> appeared to him, and, reproaching him with his base ingratitude, bade the **devil-lictors** <note>Demon attendants or guards in the underworld who carry out the sentences of the dead.</note> seize him and scald his feet in a cauldron of boiling oil. **K'u** then woke up with a start, and found that his feet were very sore and painful; and in a short time they swelled up, and his toes dropped off. Fever set in, and in his agony he shrieked out, "Ungrateful wretch that I was indeed," and fell back and expired.

### XCIII.

## HIS FATHER'S GHOST.

A man named T'ien Tzŭ-ch'êng, of Chiang-ning <note>Modern-day Nanjing.</note>, was crossing the Tung-t'ing lake <note>Dongting Lake, a large, legendary lake in Hunan province known for its sudden storms and literary associations.</note>, when the boat was capsized, and he was drowned. His son, Liang-ssŭ, who, towards the close of the Ming dynasty <note>The Ming dynasty ended in 1644; this setting suggests a time of great social and political upheaval.</note>, took the <term>highest degree</term> <note>The "Jinshi" or "Presented Scholar" degree, the peak of the Imperial examination system which guaranteed a high-ranking government position.</note>, was then a baby in arms; and his wife, hearing the bad news, swallowed poison forthwith <note>This act of suicide by a widow was historically praised in China as a "meritorious act" of extreme devotion and chastity, often resulting in the family receiving imperial honors.</note>, and left the child to the care of his grandmother. 

When Liang-ssŭ grew up, he was appointed magistrate in Hu-pei, where he remained about a year. He was then transferred to Hu-nan, on military service; but, on reaching the Tung-t'ing lake, his feelings overpowered him <note>The sight of the lake where his father died caused a psychological or emotional breakdown, a common trope of "filial piety" in Chinese literature.</note>, and he returned to plead inability as an excuse for not taking up his post. Accordingly, he was degraded to the rank of Assistant-Magistrate, which he at first declined, but was finally compelled to accept; and thenceforward gave himself up to roaming about on the lakes and

<note>⁶ Chinese dice are the exact counterpart of our own, except that the ace and the four are coloured red : the ace because the combination of black and white would be unlucky, and the four because this number once turned up in response to the call of an Emperor of the **T‘ang dynasty** <note>Likely referring to Emperor Xuanzong (r. 712–756 AD).</note>, who particularly wanted a four to win him the *partie* <note>original: "partie," meaning a match or game.</note>. All letters, despatches, and such documents, have invariably something *red* about them, this being the lucky colour, and to the Chinese, emblematic of prosperity and joy.</note>

<note>⁷ Alluding to an ancient story of a promise by a Mr. **Fan** <note>Fan Shi, a scholar of the Han Dynasty.</note> that he would return to visit his friend **Chang** <note>Zhang Shao.</note> in exactly two years. Despite the long passage of time and the distance, Fan Shi appeared on the appointed day, and Zhang’s mother, who had trusted in the promise, had a chicken dinner ready to welcome him.</note>

On arriving at home, he was unable either to eat or to sleep, so much did this affair occupy his mind; and about a year afterwards he went south again, bought a boat, and lived in it as his home, watching carefully every single vessel that passed either up or down, until at last there was hardly one he didn't know by sight. But all this time the boat he was looking for never reappeared.

<margin>
5 Witnesses in a Chinese court of justice do not take an oath in the way Westerners understand the term. Their written statements, however, always end with the phrase "the above evidence is the truth!" In daily life, people call upon heaven and earth to witness their words, or, as seen here, the sun. They may also declare themselves willing to die if they are lying. The practice of "saucer-breaking" <note>A Victorian-era myth that Chinese legal oaths involved breaking a ceramic saucer to symbolize the breaking of one's life if they lied.</note> is a misconception based on perhaps a single instance; it is not a national custom in China. "Cock-killing" usually refers to initiation rituals for secret societies, which were common throughout the Empire despite being punishable by death.
6 Adoption is common throughout China and strictly regulated by law. For example, an adopted son takes precedence over all biological daughters in inheritance. A man cannot marry a girl he has adopted until he has first "given her away" to be adopted by a family with a different surname to break the legal family bond; only after this fictional ceremony can he marry her.

### XCVI.
## A SUPERNATURAL WIFE.

A CERTAIN Mr. Chao, of Ch'ang-shan <note>Ch'ang-shan: An ancient administrative region located in modern-day Hebei Province, northern China.</note>, lodged in a family of the name of T'ai. He was very badly off, and, falling sick, was brought almost to death's door. One day they moved him into the verandah, that it might be cooler for him; and, when he awoke from a nap, lo! a beautiful girl was standing by his side. 

"I am come to be your wife," said the girl, in answer to his question as to who she was; to which he replied that a poor fellow like himself did not look for such luck as that; adding that, being then on his death-bed, he would not have much occasion for the services of a wife. The girl said she could cure him; but he told her he very much doubted that; "And even," continued he, "should you have any good prescription, I have not the means of getting it made up." 

"I don't want medicine to cure you with," rejoined the girl, proceeding at once to rub his back and sides with her hand, which seemed to him like a ball of fire <note>ball of fire: This sensation describes the transfer of *qi* (vital energy) or spiritual heat, a common motif in Chinese supernatural tales where spirits heal mortals through direct physical contact.</note>. ***

<sup>3</sup> This describes the common historical practice of repaying a loan used by an impoverished candidate to cover the costs of traveling to a new government post. These loans were typically provided by a "<term>Western merchant<note>Original text: "hsi-shang."</note></term>," a term used for a **Shanxi** banker (**Shanxi** literally means "west of the mountains"). A representative of the bank would often accompany the new official to his post, holding his official commission as collateral until the debt was paid. The official would then raise the funds, often by issuing a public decree—for example, ordering the closure of all gambling houses. The owners of these "hells" (gambling dens) would immediately send large "presents" of money to the official to stay open. The Shanxi banker would receive his principal plus high interest (sometimes 2 percent *per month*), the gambling houses would continue their business, and the official would keep the remaining profit.

### XCVIII.
## A CHINESE JONAH. <note>This title refers to the biblical story of Jonah, who was thrown overboard to calm a storm; in this version, the man cast out is the only one who survives.</note>

A man named **Sun Pi-chên** was crossing the **river**<gloss>The Yang-tsze (Yangtze): often referred to as the "Long River" in China.</gloss> when a massive thunder-squall suddenly struck the vessel. The boat began to toss violently, causing great terror among all the passengers. Just then, a heavenly being in golden armor appeared standing upon the clouds above them. In his hand, he held a scroll inscribed with characters written in gold. The people on the vessel could easily see there were three characters: **Sun Pi-chên** <note>original: "孫必振" (Sūn Bìzhèn). In Chinese naming conventions, the family name "Sun" comes first.</note>.

Turning immediately to their fellow traveler, the passengers said to him, “You have clearly angered Heaven; get into a small boat by yourself, and do not make us suffer your punishment with you.” Without giving him a moment to agree or refuse, they hurried him over the side into a small rowboat and set him adrift. But when **Sun Pi-chên** looked back, he saw that the main vessel itself had capsized.<gloss>The full irony of this story is a play on words. The man's family name was **Sun**, and his given name, **Pi-chên**, sounds exactly like the phrase "Must-be-saved." However, there is another word that sounds identical—**chên**—which means "struck" (as in struck by lightning or disaster). The other passengers heard or saw the name and mistook "Must-be-saved" for "Must-be-struck." Because of their haste to sacrifice him, they met the very fate they thought was meant for him, while Mr. Sun's little boat rode safely through the storm.</gloss>

---

<summary>A traveler named Sun Pi-chên is cast off a ship during a storm after his name appears in the sky, but the passengers' misunderstanding of his name leads them to their own deaths while he is saved.</summary>

## XCIX.

### CHANG PU-LIANG <note>The name is a play on words. While "Chang" is the family name, "Pu-liang" sounds identical to two different phrases: one meaning "wicked" and the other meaning "not measuring."</note>

A certain trader who was travelling in the province of **Chih-li** <gloss>Zhili: A historical province in northern China, mostly corresponding to modern-day Hebei province.</gloss>, being overtaken by a storm of rain and hail, took shelter among some standing crops by the way-side. There he heard a voice from heaven, saying, “These are **Chang Pu-liang’s** fields; do not injure his crops.” The trader began to wonder who this **Chang Pu-liang** could be, and how, if he was *pu liang* <note>original: "不良" (bù liáng), meaning "not good" or "wicked."</note> (**not virtuous**), he came to be under **divine protection**; so when the storm was over and he had reached the neighbouring village, he made enquiries on the subject, and told the people there what he had heard. The villagers then informed him that **Chang Pu-liang** was a very wealthy farmer, who was accustomed every spring to make loans of grain to the poor of the district, and who was not too particular about getting back the exact amount he had lent,—taking, in fact, whatever they brought him without discussion; hence the **sobriquet** <term>sobriquet: a nickname or descriptive name.</term> of *pu liang* <note>original: "不量" (bù liáng), meaning "not measuring" or "without a gauge."</note> (**“no measure”**) <gloss>referring to the man who does not measure the repayments of his loans</gloss>.¹

<note>¹ Here again we have a play upon words similar to that in the last story. In Chinese, many different characters share the same sound, leading to frequent misunderstandings or clever puns in folk tales.</note>

## 102.

### A TAOIST DEVOTEE

CHÜ YAO-JU was a man from Ch‘ing-chou <note>Ch‘ing-chou (modern Qingzhou) in Shandong province was an area rich in history and religious tradition during the Qing Dynasty.</note> who, upon the death of his wife, decided to leave his secular life behind and become a priest. <note>The author notes it was more common for a widower to "renew the guitar string," a Chinese idiom meaning to remarry. The *Sacred Edict* (a set of imperial moral guidelines) taught that the bond between brothers was more vital than that between husband and wife, as a wife could be replaced through remarriage, but a brother could not.</note> Several years later, he returned to his home village dressed in the traditional robes of a Taoist. He carried a meditation mat <note>The original text uses "praying-mat." In this context, it refers to a portable mat used for sitting in meditation or prayer.</note> over his shoulder. After staying for only one night, he prepared to depart once more.

His friends, however, were unwilling to let him leave and withheld his <term>cassock</term> <note>A long, ceremonial robe worn by clergy.</note> and his traveling staff. To trick them, he pretended to take a simple walk outside the village walls. As soon as he was outside, his clothes and other belongings suddenly flew out of the house through the air, following him of their own accord. With his possessions returned to him by magic, he was able to make his escape safely. <note>The author points out that both the staff and the meditation mat mentioned are traditionally associated with Buddhism, even though the protagonist is described as a Taoist, illustrating the frequent blending of religious symbols in popular Chinese folk stories.</note>

### 103.

### JUSTICE FOR REBELS.

DURING the reign of the Emperor Shunzhi <note>Original: "Shun Chih." The first Manchu ruler of the Qing dynasty, who ascended the throne in 1644.</note>, seventy percent of the people in Teng-yi <note>Original: "T‘êng-i." A district in Shandong province.</note> were opposed to the newly established Manchu dynasty. The government officials dared not touch them; and later, when the country became more settled, the magistrates used to distinguish these people from the others by always deciding any legal cases in their favour. This was done out of fear that these men might revert to their old opposition against the state.

And thus it came about that every litigant would begin their case by declaring themselves to have been a "rebel," while his adversary would follow up by trying to show that such a statement was false. As a result, before any case could even be heard on its actual merits, it was necessary for the court to determine the political status of both the plaintiff and the defendant. This created a massive amount of extra work for the Registrars <note>The officials responsible for maintaining court records and legal documents.</note>.

Now it chanced that the <term>yamên</term> <note>The administrative office and residence of a local government official.</note> of one of the officials was haunted by a fox spirit, and the official's daughter was—

Regarding <note>original: "Apropos"</note> this passage, Ibn Battuta <note>The 14th-century Moroccan scholar and traveler who recorded seeing a similar "rope trick" in China.</note> writes as follows:—"They produced a chain fifty cubits in length, and in my presence threw one end of it towards the sky, where it remained, as if fastened to something in the air. A dog was then brought forward, and, being placed at the lower end of the chain, immediately ran up, and reaching the other end immediately disappeared in the air. In the same manner a hog, a panther, a lion, and a tiger were alternately sent up the chain, and all equally disappeared at the upper end of it. At last they took down the chain, and put it into a bag, no one ever discerning in what way the different animals were made to vanish into the air in the mysterious manner above described. This, I may venture to affirm, was beyond measure strange and surprising."

Concerning this passage, Mr. Maskelyne <note>John Nevil Maskelyne, a famous Victorian stage magician and inventor known for debunking fraudulent supernatural claims.</note>, the prince of all black-artists <term>black-artists<gloss>A historical term for stage magicians or illusionists, not necessarily implying "dark magic."</gloss></term>, ancient or modern, says:—"These apparent effects were, doubtless, due to the aid of concave mirrors, the use of which was known to the ancients, especially in the East, but they could not have been produced in the open air."

### CV.
## KILLING A SERPENT.

On Ku-chi island <note>original: "Ku-chi" — Likely a fictional or remote island in the East China Sea, possibly based on the Zhoushan archipelago.</note> in the eastern sea, there were camellias of all colours which bloomed throughout the year. No one, however, lived there, and very few people ever visited the spot. One day, a young man of Têng-chou <note>original: "Têng-chou" — Modern-day Penglai in Shandong Province, historically a famous port and home to legends of the Eight Immortals.</note>, named Chang <note>Zhang</note>, who was fond of hunting and adventure, hearing of the beauties of the place, put together some wine and food, and rowed himself across in a small open boat. 

The flowers were just then even finer than usual, and their perfume was diffused for a mile or so around; while many of the trees he saw were several <term>armfuls in circumference<gloss>In Chinese measurement, a "wei" is the span of a person's outstretched arms, used to describe the girth of ancient trees.</gloss></term>. So he roamed about and gave himself up to enjoyment of the scene; and by-and-by he opened a flask of wine, regretting very much that he had no companion to share it with him, when all of a sudden a most beautiful young girl, with extremely bright eyes and dressed in red, stepped down from one of the camellias before him. <note>The author likely references a previous note (Story 71, note 6) which discusses the folklore of flower spirits or tree-dwelling nymphs appearing to solitary travelers.</note> “Dear me!” said she on seeing Mr. Chang; “I expected to be alone here, and did not know that a gentleman was coming to visit us.”

## 106.

# THE RESUSCITATED CORPSE

An old man lived in <term>Ts‘ai-tien</term><note>A village in the Shandong province area.</note>, in the <term>Yang-hsin district</term>. The village was located some miles from the district city, and he and his son kept a roadside inn where travellers could pass the night. 

One day, as it was getting dusk, four strangers presented themselves and asked for a night’s lodging; to which the landlord replied that every bed was already occupied. The four men declared it was impossible for them to go back, and urged him to take them in somehow; and at length the landlord said he could give them a place to sleep in if they were not too particular—which the strangers immediately assured him they were not. 

The fact was that the old man’s daughter-in-law had just died, and that her body was lying in the <term>women’s quarters</term><note>The private inner rooms of a traditional Chinese house, usually reserved for the family's female members and closed to outsiders.</note>, waiting for the coffin, which his son had gone away to buy. So the landlord led them round thither, and walking in, placed a lamp on the table. At the further end of the room lay the corpse, decked out with <term>paper robes</term><note>original: "chih-yi" — Ceremonial garments made of paper used in funeral rites to clothe the dead for the afterlife.</note>, etc., in the usual way; and in the foremost section were sleeping-couches for four people. ### CVII.

## THE FISHERMAN AND HIS FRIEND.

IN the northern parts of Tzŭ-chou <note>Tzŭ-chou (Zizhou) was a historical department in China, located in what is now the Sichuan province.</note> there lived a man named Hsü, a fisherman by trade. Every night when he went to fish he would carry some wine with him, and drink and fish by turns, always taking care to pour out a libation <note>A ritual pouring of wine as an offering to the deceased or to spirits.</note> on the ground, accompanied by the following invocation—"Drink too, ye drowned spirits of the river!" <note>original: "河中溺鬼飲之！" These are the *shui gui* or "water ghosts," spirits of those who drowned and are believed to remain in the water until they can find a replacement.</note> Such was his regular custom; and it was also noticeable that, even on occasions when the other fishermen caught nothing, he always got a full basket. One night, as he was sitting drinking by himself, a young man suddenly appeared and began walking up and down near him. Hsü offered him a cup of wine, which was readily accepted, and they remained chatting together throughout the night, Hsü meanwhile not catching a single fish. However, just as he was giving up all hope of doing anything, the young man rose and said he would go a little way down the stream and beat them up <note>A technique of splashing or making noise to drive fish toward a net.</note> towards Hsü, which he accordingly did, returning in a few minutes and warning him to be on the look-out. Hsü now heard a noise like that of a shoal <note>A large group or school of fish.</note> coming up the stream, and, casting his net, made a splendid haul,—all that he caught being over a foot in length. ² This story reflects a well-known and often criticized reluctance among some people to save drowning strangers. ### CVIII.

## THE PRIEST’S WARNING.

A MAN named **Chang** <note>original: "Chang"; one of the most common Chinese surnames, used here as a generic "everyman" protagonist.</note> died suddenly, and was escorted at once by **devil-lictors** <note>original: "guiyi"; these are spiritual bailiffs or "police" of the underworld. In Chinese folklore, the afterlife is a vast bureaucracy where spirits are arrested with formal warrants just like in the living world.</note> into the presence of the **King of Purgatory** <note>original: "Yanluo Wang"; the ruler of the underworld and judge of the dead, adapted from the Buddhist figure Yama.</note>. His Majesty turned to Chang’s record of good and evil, and then, in great anger, told the lictors they had brought the wrong man, and bade them take him back again. 

As they left the judgment-hall, Chang persuaded his escort to let him have a look at Purgatory; and, accordingly, the devils conducted him through the **nine sections** <note>original: "jiu you" or the Nine Dark Places. This traditional Chinese conception of the underworld mirrors the nine circles or "bolgie" of the Inferno described by Dante Alighieri.</note>, pointing out to him the **Knife Hill** <note>original: "Dao Shan"; a terrifying cliff where sinners are thrown onto sharp, upright blades.</note>, the **Sword Tree** <note>original: "Jian Shu"; a tree with branches made of razor-sharp blades that lacerate those who pass by.</note>, and other objects of interest. By-and-by, they reached a place where there was a Buddhist priest, hanging suspended in the air head downwards, by a rope through a hole in his leg.

<summary>A man named Chang is accidentally taken to the underworld, where he is granted a tour of the various chambers of punishment before his soul is returned to his body.</summary>

Chang now told him what he had seen in **Purgatory**, at which the priest was so terrified, that he at once gave up taking **wine and meat** <note>Strict adherence to Mahayana Buddhist vows in China requires a vegetarian diet and total abstinence from alcohol.</note>, and devoted himself entirely to religious exercises. In a fortnight he was well, and was known ever afterwards as a most exemplary priest.

As the story goes, it matters little if the spirits drink much or little; however, if stubborn souls refuse to drink, sharp blades spring up beneath their feet and a copper tube is forced down their throats to compel them to swallow the brew.</note>

## CX.

## THE FORTY STRINGS OF CASH.

MR. JUSTICE WANG <note>Likely referring to a local magistrate or high-ranking official. In the original Chinese context, these stories often featured real-life officials to add a sense of historical weight.</note> had a steward, who was possessed of considerable means. One night the latter dreamt that a man rushed in and said to him, “To-day you must repay me those forty strings of cash <term>strings of cash<gloss>In ancient China, copper coins had square holes in the center and were strung together on cords. One "string" (or *diao*) usually consisted of 1,000 coins.</gloss></term>.” The steward asked who he was; to which the man made no answer, but hurried past him into the women’s apartments. When the steward awoke, he found that his wife had been delivered of a son; and, knowing at once that retribution <note>original: *baoying*—the Buddhist and Taoist concept of cosmic cause and effect, or karma. Here, it specifically refers to the "debt-collecting" reincarnation.</note> was at hand, he set aside forty strings of cash to be spent solely in food, clothes, medicines, and so on, for the baby. 

By the time the child was between three and four years old, the steward found that of the forty strings only about seven hundred cash remained; and when the wet-nurse, who happened to be standing by, brought the child and dandled it in her arms before him, he looked at it and said, “The forty strings are all but repaid; it is time you were off again.” Thereupon the child changed colour; its head fell back, and its eyes stared fixedly, and, when they tried to revive it, lo! respiration had already ceased. The father then took the balance of the forty strings,

Formerly, an old childless man consulted a great many <term>Buddhist priests<gloss>Monks who were frequently consulted in traditional Chinese society as spiritual advisors and experts on the laws of karma and reincarnation.</gloss></term> on the subject. One of them said to him,

### CXI.

## SAVING LIFE.

A CERTAIN gentleman of <term>Shên-yu<gloss>Likely referring to Shenyu County in Shanxi province.</gloss></term>, who had taken the <term>highest degree<gloss>The *jinshi* or "presented scholar" degree, the highest level of the imperial examination system, which qualified a man for high government office.</gloss></term>, could remember himself in a previous state of existence. He said he had formerly been a scholar, and had died in middle life; and that when he appeared before the <term>Judge of Purgatory<gloss>In Chinese folk religion, the afterlife is a bureaucratic system where the "Judge" (often Yanluo Wang) weighs a person's good and evil deeds to determine their next life.</gloss></term>, there stood the cauldrons, the boiling oil, and other apparatus of torture, exactly as we read about them on earth. In the eastern corner of the hall were a number of frames from which hung the skins of sheep, dogs, oxen, horses, etc.; and when anybody was condemned to reappear in life under any one of these forms, his skin was stripped off and a skin was taken from the proper frame and fixed on to his body. <note>Traditional Chinese folklore describes reincarnation into animal form as a physical transformation performed by underworld attendants using these skins.</note>

The gentleman of whom I am writing heard himself sentenced to become a sheep; and the attendant devils had already clothed him in a sheep’s-skin in the manner above described, when the clerk of the record informed the Judge that the criminal before him had once saved another man’s life.
