### 112.

## THE SALT SMUGGLER.

Wang Shi, of Gaowan <note>modern Pinyin: Kao-wan</note>, was a petty salt huckster <term>huckster: a traveling vendor or peddler, often of small or cheap goods</term> who was inordinately fond of gambling. One night he was arrested by two men, whom he took for officers of the Salt Tax Department <note>original: "Salt Gabelle," a term derived from the French word for a salt tax</note>; and, flinging down what salt he had with him, he tried to make his escape.¹ He found, however, that his legs would not move with him, and he was—

---

¹ Salt was a government monopoly in China, and its sale was only permitted to licensed dealers. It was a prohibited article of trade, whether for import or export, for foreign nations trading with China. <note>In an account of a journey from Shantou <gloss>Swatow</gloss> to Guangzhou <gloss>Canton</gloss> in March-April, 1877, the author wrote: "Speaking of salt, we came across a large hidden compartment of it when stowing away our things below the deck. The boatmen could not resist the temptation of doing a little smuggling on the way up. At a secluded point in a bamboo-shaded bend of the river, they ran the boat alongside the bank and were instantly met by a number of suspicious-looking men with baskets, who soon relieved them of the smuggled salt and went their separate ways."</note> This illustrates how the people of China sought to lighten the heavy pressure of this tax. A curious custom also existed in Guangzhou <gloss>Canton</gloss>: certain blind elderly men and women were allowed to sell salt on the streets to earn a meager living from the small profits.

It may interest readers to know that in the cities of northern China, **ice** and **coal** could only be sold by licensed dealers. These dealers were granted their licenses on the condition that they supply the *yamens* <term>yamen: the administrative office or residence of a local government official</term> of the local officials <gloss>mandarins</gloss> with these two necessities free of charge.

² The Styx <note>original: "Styx," the river of the dead in Greek mythology. The translator uses this western term to refer to the Chinese *Naihe*, or the River of Helplessness, which souls must cross</note>.
³ These words require some explanation. Ordinarily they would be taken in the sense of casting **cash** <term>cash: the standard copper currency of imperial China, notable for the square hole in the center used for stringing coins together</term> of a base description ; but they might equally well signify the casting of iron articles of any kind, and thereby hang some curious details. Iron foundries in China may only be opened under license from the local officials, and the articles there made, consisting chiefly of cooking utensils, may only be sold within a given area, each district having its own particular foundries from which alone the supplies of the neighbourhood may be derived. Free trade in iron is much feared by the authorities, as thereby pirates and rebels would be enabled to supply themselves with arms. At the framing of the Treaty of Tientsin <note>A significant 1858 treaty between the Qing Dynasty and foreign powers, including Britain and France</note>, with its accompanying tariff and rules, iron was not specified among other prohibited articles of commerce. Consequently, British merchants would appear to have a full right to purchase iron in the interior and convey it to any of the open ports under Transit-pass <note>A permit that allowed foreign goods to be transported inland without paying multiple local taxes</note>. But the Chinese officials steadily refuse to acknowledge, or permit the exercise of, this right, putting forward their own time-honoured custom with regard to iron, and enumerating the disadvantages to China were such an innovation to be brought about.

## CXIII.

### COLLECTING SUBSCRIPTIONS.

The <term>Frog-God: known in Chinese as Ha Wang, this deity was widely worshipped in parts of Imperial China, particularly in areas like Henan. Followers believed the god could influence the weather, health, and local prosperity.</term> frequently employs a magician to deliver its oracles to those who have faith. Should the magician declare that the God is pleased, happiness is sure to follow; but if he says the God is angry, women and children <note>original: "The chief supporters of superstition in China." All this time the magician had been in a divine ecstasy <note>The "divine ecstasy" refers to a state of spirit possession or trance where the medium's own consciousness is replaced by that of the deity.</note>, not knowing what he was saying; and when he came round, and was told what had happened, his shame knew no bounds, so he pawned some of his clothes, and paid in the balance of his own debt. As to the two defaulters who did not pay, one of them was ill for a month and more; while the other had a bad attack of boils.

# 117.

## THE INVISIBLE PRIEST.

Mr. Han was a gentleman from a family of high social standing. He was on very intimate terms with a skilled Taoist priest and magician named Tan, who possessed a remarkable talent: while sitting among a group of guests, he could suddenly make himself invisible. Mr. Han was extremely anxious to learn this magic art, but Tan refused all his pleading.

"It is not," Tan explained, "because I want to keep the secret for myself, but simply as a matter of principle. To teach the <term>superior man</term> <note>original: "junzi" (君子). In Confucian ethics, this refers to a person of high moral integrity and self-cultivation.</note> would be well enough; others, however, would use such knowledge to rob their neighbors. There is no fear that you would do this, though even you might be tempted in certain ways."

->CXVIII.<-

## THE CENSOR IN PURGATORY

Just beyond **Fengdu** <note>original: "Fêng-tu." A city in modern-day Chongqing famous in Chinese mythology as the "City of Ghosts" and the entrance to the underworld.</note> there is a fathomless cave which is reputed to be the entrance to **the Netherworld** <note>original: "Purgatory." Giles uses this Western term for the Chinese *Diyu*, the realm of the dead where souls are judged and punished.</note>. All the implements of torture employed therein are of human manufacture; old, worn-out shackles and fetters are occasionally found at the mouth of the cave, and are regularly replaced by new ones. These disappear the same night, and the magistrate of the district includes the cost as a formal charge in his official accounts. <note>Giles notes that this refers to a common practice where local officials would embezzle funds under the guise of providing supplies for the spirit world.</note>

Under the **Ming dynasty** <note>The ruling dynasty of China from 1368 to 1644.</note>, there was a certain **Censor** <note>original: "Censor." A high-ranking official in the Censorate, an imperial oversight agency responsible for investigating corruption and maintaining government integrity.</note>,

---

<note>original footnote 1</note> **Fengdu** is a district city in the province of **Sichuan** <note>original: "Szechuen."</note>, and near it are said to be "fire-wells" <note>Natural gas vents that have burned for centuries, often associated with the heat of the underworld.</note>, otherwise known as the entrance to the Netherworld, the capital city of which is also called Fengdu.

<note>original footnote 2</note> This charge is made to the **Imperial Treasury**. From what I know of the shamelessness of similar official frauds, I should say that this statement is quite within the bounds of truth. For instance, at **Xiamen** <note>original: "Amoy."</note> one percent is collected by the local officials on all imports, ostensibly for the purpose of providing the Emperor’s table with a delicious kind of **edible bird’s nest** said to be found in the neighborhood! Seventy percent of the sum thus collected is pocketed by the various officials of the place, and with the remaining thirty percent a certain quantity of the ordinary commercial article is imported from **the Malay Peninsula** <note>original: "the Straits."</note> and forwarded to **Beijing** <note>original: "Peking."</note>.

### CXXII.

## THE FLYING COW.

### CXXIII.

## THE “MIRROR AND LISTEN” TRICK.

At I-tu <note>I-tu is a district in the Shandong province of China.</note> there lived a family of the name of Chêng. The two sons were both distinguished scholars, but the elder was early known to fame, and, consequently, the favourite with his parents, who also extended their preference to his wife. The younger brother was a trifle wild, which displeased his father and mother very much, and made them regard his wife, too, with anything but a friendly eye. The latter reproached her husband for being the cause of this, and asked him why he, being a man like his brother, could not vindicate the slights that were put upon her. This piqued him; and, setting to work in good earnest, he soon gained a fair reputation, though still not equal to his brother’s. That year the two went up for the highest degree <term>highest degree: the *jinshi* (presented scholar) degree, the most prestigious level of the Imperial civil service examinations</term>; and, on New Year’s Eve, the wife of the younger, very anxious for the success of her husband, secretly tried the “mirror and listen” trick. <note>original: *jingting*; a form of folk divination. One method is to wrap an old mirror—formerly a polished metal disc—in a handkerchief, and then, while alone, bow seven times towards the Spirit of the Hearth <term>Spirit of the Hearth: the Kitchen God, a deity who resides in the kitchen and monitors the family's deeds</term>. After this ritual, the first words heard spoken by any person in the street are believed to provide a clue or omen regarding the person's future success or failure.</note> She saw

### CXXV.

## THE MARRIAGE OF THE VIRGIN GODDESS.

At Kuei-chi <note>Modern-day Shaoxing in Zhejiang province</note> there is a shrine dedicated to the **Plum Virgin**, who was once a young lady from the Ma family living in Tung-wan. When her betrothed husband died before their wedding day, she took a sacred vow never to marry anyone else. She passed away at the age of thirty. Her relatives built a shrine in her memory and honored her with the title of the **Plum Virgin**. 

Some years later, a scholar named Mr. Chin, who was traveling to take the <term>examination|The Imperial civil service examinations, which were the primary route to social status and government office in old China</term>, happened to pass by the shrine. Upon entering, he walked back and forth through the halls, his mind deeply occupied with thoughts of the virtuous young woman to whom the temple was dedicated. 

That night, he had a dream in which a servant arrived to summon him into the presence of the Goddess. Following the command, he went and found her waiting for him just outside the shrine. 

"I am deeply grateful to you, Sir," the Goddess said as he approached, "for giving me so large a share of your thoughts; and I intend to repay you by becoming your <term>humble handmaid|A traditional, modest way for a woman to refer to herself as a prospective wife in this period</term>." 

Mr. Chin bowed to show his agreement. The Goddess then escorted him back, saying, "When your place is ready, I will come and fetch you." Upon waking in the—

### CXXVI.

## THE WINE INSECT.

A MR. LIN of Ch'ang-shan <note>A historical county in Zhejiang province, China</note> was extremely fat, and so fond of wine<gloss>1</gloss> that he would often finish a pitcher by himself. However, he owned about fifty acres of land, half of which was covered with millet <note>Millet was a primary grain used for fermenting and distilling spirits in northern China</note>, and being well off, he did not consider that his drinking would bring him into trouble. 

One day a foreign Buddhist priest <note>In traditional Chinese tales, "foreign" monks—often from India or Central Asia—were frequently depicted as possessing mystical medical or exorcism powers</note> saw him, and remarked that he appeared to be suffering from some extraordinary complaint. Mr. Lin said nothing was the matter with him; whereupon the priest asked him if he often got drunk. Lin acknowledged that he did; and the priest told him that he was afflicted by the **wine insect** <note>In Chinese folklore, certain cravings were believed to be caused by literal "insects" or parasites inside the body that consumed the essence of the substance the person craved</note>. 

"Dear me!" cried Lin, in great alarm, "do you think you could cure me?" The priest declared there would be no difficulty in doing so; but when Lin asked him what drugs he intended to use, the priest said he should not use any at all. He then made Lin lie down in the sun; and tying his hands and feet together, he placed a stoup <note>A flagon or vessel for liquor</note> of good wine about—

# CXXVIII.

## AN EARTHQUAKE.

IN 1668 there was a very severe earthquake. <note>original: "the 17th of the 6th moon" (July 25, 1668). This was the Great Tancheng earthquake, estimated at magnitude 8.5, the strongest ever recorded in Eastern China.</note> I myself was staying at Chi-hsia <note>Now known as Qixia, a city in the Shandong province.</note>, and happened to be that night sitting over a kettle of wine with my cousin Li Tu. All of a sudden we heard a noise like thunder, travelling from the south-east in a north-westerly direction. We were much astonished at this, and quite unable to account for the noise ; in another moment the table began to rock, and the wine-cups were upset ; the beams and supports of the house snapped here and there with a crash, and we looked at each other in fear and trembling. By-and-by we knew that it was an earthquake ; and, rushing out, we saw houses and other buildings, as it were, fall down and get up again <note>This vividly describes the "rolling" motion of the ground during high-magnitude seismic waves.</note> ; and, amidst the sounds of crushing walls, we heard the shrieks of women and children, the whole mass being like a great seething cauldron. Men were giddy and could not stand, but rolled about on the ground ; the river overflowed its banks ;

### CXXIX.

## MAKING ANIMALS.

The tricks for bewitching people are many. Sometimes drugs are put in their food, and when they eat they become dazed, and follow the person who has bewitched them. This is commonly called *ta hsü pa* <note>original: "ta hsü pa" (daxuba). A historical term for a type of kidnapping involving stupefying drugs.</note>; in Kiang-nan <note>original: "Kiang-nan" (Jiangnan). A region south of the Yangtze River known for its prosperity and culture.</note> it is known as *ch‘ê hsü* <note>original: "ch‘ê hsü" (chexu). A regional dialect term for the same deceptive practices.</note>. Little children are most frequently bewitched in this way. There is also what is called “making animals,” which is better known on the south side of the River.^1 <note>Referring to the Yangtze River.</note>

One day a man arrived at an inn in Yang-chow <note>original: "Yang-chow" (Yangzhou). A major historical city in Jiangsu province.</note>, leading with him five donkeys. Tying them up near the stable, he told the landlord he would be back in a few minutes, and bade him give his donkeys no water. He had not been gone long before the donkeys, which were standing out in the glare of the sun, began to kick about, and make a noise; whereupon the landlord untied them, and was going to put them in the shade, when suddenly they espied water, and made a rush to get at it. So the landlord let them drink; and no sooner had the water touched their lips than they rolled

# CXXX.

## CRUELTY AVENGED.

A certain <term>magistrate</term> <note>A local official acting as both judge and administrator of a county.</note> caused a petty oil-vendor, who was brought before him for some trifling misdemeanour, and whose statements were very confused, to be <term>bambooed</term> <note>original: "bambooed to death"; a common but brutal form of corporal punishment in imperial China using heavy bamboo poles.</note> to death. The former subsequently rose to high rank; and having amassed considerable wealth, set about building himself a fine house. On the day when the great beam was to be fixed in its place <note>The "fixing of the beam" was a major ritual in Chinese construction, similar to the Western "topping out" ceremony or laying a foundation stone, marking the completion of the building's frame.</note>, among the friends and relatives who arrived to offer their congratulations, he was horrified to see the oilman walk in. At the same instant one of the servants came rushing up to announce to him the birth of a son; whereupon, he mournfully remarked, "The house not yet finished, and its destroyer already here." The bystanders thought he was joking, for they had not seen what he had seen <note>The magistrate saw the disembodied spirit of the murdered oil-vendor entering the house to be reborn as his son.</note>. However, when that boy grew up, by his frivolity and extravagance he quite ruined his father. He was finally obliged himself to go into service; and spent all his earnings in oil, which he swallowed in large quantities.

---

| Word | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Magistrate** | A government official who served as the local judge. |
| **Oil-vendor** | A street merchant who sold cooking oil, often a symbol of a common, hardworking citizen. |
| **Bambooed** | To be beaten with a heavy split bamboo; often a fatal punishment if excessive. |
| **Great Beam** | The main horizontal support of a roof, central to traditional Chinese architecture. |
| **Retribution** | The idea that one's bad deeds will return to punish them, often in a future life. |

### 132.

# THE FORTUNE-HUNTER PUNISHED.

A certain man’s uncle had no children, and the nephew, with an eye to his uncle’s property, volunteered to become his **adopted son**. <note>In traditional Chinese society, adoption was primarily a formal arrangement to ensure a childless man would have a male heir to perform "ancestral worship"—the essential rites and offerings required for a soul's peace in the afterlife.</note> When the uncle died, all the property passed accordingly to his nephew, who thereupon broke faith as to his part of the contract. <note>Specifically, he failed to perform the funerary obligations he had promised, such as conducting the seasonal ceremonies and repairing the family tombs.</note> He did the same with another uncle, and thus united three properties in his own person, whereby he became the richest man of the neighborhood. 

Suddenly he fell ill and seemed to go out of his mind; for he cried out, “So you wish to live in wealth, do you?” and immediately seizing a sharp knife, he began hacking away at his own body until he had strewed the floor with pieces of flesh. He then exclaimed, “You cut off other people’s **posterity** <note>Meaning his descendants or bloodline. By failing to honor his adoption, he effectively ended his uncles' spiritual lineages.</note> and expect to have posterity yourself, do you?” and forthwith he ripped himself open and died. Shortly afterwards his son, too, died, and the property fell into the hands of strangers. Is not this a **retribution** <term>retribution</term> <note>The concept of *baoying*, or karmic justice, which suggests that the universe naturally balances moral debts, often through poetic or ironic punishment.</note> to be dreaded?

<summary>This story warns against greed and the betrayal of family obligations. A man who tricks his childless uncles to inherit their wealth is driven to a gruesome suicide by supernatural forces, ensuring his own lineage is wiped out as punishment.</summary>

<keywords>adoption, ancestral worship, inheritance, greed, karma, retribution, filial piety, family lineage</keywords>

## CXXXIV.

### THE CLAY IMAGE.

On the **Yi River** <note>original: "river I"; the Yi River in Shandong province is the setting for many of these tales.</note> there lived a man named **Ma**, who married a woman from the **Wang** family. They were very happy in their life together. However, Ma died while he was still young. His wife’s parents were unwilling to let their daughter remain a widow, but she resisted all their persistent demands and declared firmly that she would never marry again. 

“I admit your resolution is noble,” her mother argued, “but you are still just a girl and you have no children. Besides, I have noticed that people who start with such rigid determination often end up doing something shameful. You would be better off getting married as soon as you can—it is no more than what people do every day.” The daughter swore she would rather die than give her consent, so her mother had no choice but to leave her alone. 

The woman then ordered a **clay image** <term>a lifelike figurine or statue made of clay, common in folk traditions for commemorating the deceased</term> to be made that looked exactly like her late husband;¹ and whenever she sat down for her own meals, she

They find it more difficult, however, to capture foreign faces, as they are less accustomed to them.</note>

->FROM A CHINESE STUDIO.<-

During the investigation, the **magistrate** <note>In imperial China, a magistrate acted as the local judge, governor, and police chief for a district.</note> exclaimed, “I have heard that the children of **disembodied spirits** <note>original: *gui*; ghosts or spirits of the deceased.</note> have no shadow; and that those who have shadows are not genuine.” Thereupon they took Ma’s child into the sunshine, and lo! there was but a very faint shadow, like a thin vapour.

The magistrate then drew blood from the child, and smeared it on the clay image; upon which the blood at once soaked in and left no stain. Another clay image being produced and the same experiment tried, the blood remained on the surface so that it could be wiped away.⁴ <margin>⁴ Such is the officially authorised method of determining a doubtful relationship between a dead parent and a living child, substituting a bone for the clay image here mentioned. <note>This refers to the ancient forensic practice of *dixue renqin* (blood-dripping to recognize kin). It was believed that a child's blood would soak into the bone of a biological parent but bead off the bone of a stranger.</note></margin> The girl’s story was thus acknowledged to be true; and when the child grew up, and in every feature was the counterpart of Ma, there was no longer any room for suspicion.

<summary>The magistrate uses supernatural and traditional forensic tests—examining the child's shadow and performing a blood-affinity test on the clay statue—to prove the child is the legitimate son of the deceased Ma. The story concludes with the child growing up to perfectly resemble his father, vindicating the widow's miraculous claims.</summary>

### CXXXV.

## DISHONESTY PUNISHED.

At Chiao-chou <note>Modern Jiaozhou, a city in Shandong Province.</note> there lived a man named Liu Hsi-ch'uan <note>Pinyin: Liu Xichuan.</note>, who was steward to His excellency Mr. Fa. # CXXXVI.

## THE MAD PRIEST.

A certain mad priest, whose name I do not know, lived in a temple on the hills. He would sing and cry by turns, without any apparent reason; and once somebody saw him boiling a stone for his dinner. <note>In Chinese folklore, "boiling stones" is a common trope for an enlightened being or immortal who has transcended the need for ordinary food, often associated with the practice of internal alchemy.</note> At the autumn festival of the 9th day of the 9th moon,¹ <note>original: "9th day of the 9th moon". This refers to the Double Ninth Festival (Chongyang), a holiday where people climb mountains to avoid bad luck and enjoy the autumn scenery.</note> an official of the district went up in that direction for the usual picnic, taking with him his chair <note>A sedan chair or palanquin, the standard transport for imperial officials.</note> and his red umbrellas. <note>Red umbrellas were part of the formal regalia of a high-ranking official, used to signify their rank and authority during processions.</note> After luncheon he was passing by the temple, and had hardly reached the door, when out rushed the priest, barefooted and ragged, and himself opening a yellow umbrella, <note>Yellow was the imperial color, strictly reserved for the Emperor or high religious figures; the priest using it here is a provocative and supernatural act.</note> cried out as the attendants of a <term>mandarin</term> <note>mandarin: A term used by Westerners to describe the scholar-officials of the Chinese imperial civil service.</note> do when ordering the people to stand back. He then approached the official, and made as though he were jesting at him; at which the latter was extremely indignant, and bade his servants drive the priest away. The priest moved off with the servants after him, and in another moment had thrown down his yellow umbrella, which split into a number of pieces, each piece changing immediately into a falcon, and flying about in all directions. The umbrella handle became a huge serpent,

# CXXXIX.

## THE BUTTERFLY'S REVENGE.

MR. WANG, of <note>original: "Ch'ang-shan" — Changshan is a county in the western part of Zhejiang province, China.</note> Changshan, was in the habit, when serving as a <term>District Magistrate <gloss>the primary administrative and judicial official responsible for a local county</gloss></term>, of commuting the fines and penalties of the Penal Code inflicted on various prisoners for a corresponding number of butterflies. These he would let go all at once in the court, rejoicing to see them fluttering hither and thither, like so many tinsel snippings borne about by the breeze. 

One night he dreamt that a young lady, dressed in gay-colored clothes, appeared to him and said, “Your cruel practice has brought many of my sisters to an untimely end, and now you shall pay the penalty for thus gratifying your tastes.” <note>While Wang thought he was being kind by releasing the butterflies, the act of capturing so many for his amusement likely resulted in many of the delicate insects being crushed or dying in captivity.</note> The young lady then changed into a butterfly and flew away. 

Next day, the magistrate was sitting alone, over a cup of wine, when it was announced to him that the <term>Censor <gloss>a high-ranking imperial official whose duty was to investigate and report misconduct or corruption among other officials</gloss></term> was at the door; and out he ran at once to receive **His Excellency**, with a white flower, that some of his women had put in his official hat, still sticking there. <note>In the strict atmosphere of Imperial Chinese bureaucracy, wearing a decorative flower—especially a white one, which was associated with mourning—on an official uniform was considered a sign of extreme levity or disrespect.</note> 

**His Excellency** was very angry at what he deemed a piece of disrespect to himself; and, after severely censuring Mr. Wang, turned round and went away. Thenceforward no more penalties were commuted for butterflies.

### CXL.

## THE DOCTOR.

A CERTAIN poor man, named Chang, who lived at I <note>original: "I" — This refers to Yi County in Shandong province, China, where the author Pu Songling spent much of his life.</note>, fell in one day with a **Taoist priest** <gloss>a practitioner of the Taoist religion, frequently depicted in folk tales as having supernatural insight or mastery over the arts of divination and health</gloss>. The latter was highly skilled in the science of **physiognomy** <term>physiognomy <gloss>the historical practice of determining a person's character, personality, or future prospects based on their facial features and physical appearance</gloss></term>; <note>In traditional Chinese society, practitioners of physiognomy were common in city streets, offering to read a person’s destiny for a fee.</note> and, after looking at Chang's features, said to him, "You would make your fortune as a doctor." "Alas!" replied Chang, "I can barely read and write; how then could I follow such a calling as that." "And where, you simple fellow," asked the priest, "is the necessity for a doctor to be a scholar? You just try, that's all."

Thereupon Chang returned home; and, being very poor, he simply collected a few of the commonest prescriptions, and set up a small stall with a handful of fishes' teeth and some dry honeycomb from a wasp's nest <note>Chang displayed these odd items to create a professional appearance and impress potential patients with a "show" of exotic medicine, despite his lack of training.</note>, hoping thus to earn, by his tongue, enough to keep body and soul together, to which, how-

When Chang heard of his appointment, he happened to be suffering himself from a bad attack of **bronchitis**, which he was quite unable to cure, and he begged, therefore, to be excused; but the magistrate would not hear of this, and forwarded him at once in charge of some constables.

While crossing the hills, he became very thirsty, and went into a village to ask for a drink of water; but **water there was worth its weight in jade** <note>An idiomatic way of describing a severe drought or extreme scarcity where a basic necessity becomes as precious as a gemstone.</note>, and no one would give him any. By-and-by he saw an old woman washing a quantity of vegetables in a scanty supply of water which was, consequently, very thick and muddy; and, being unable to bear his thirst any longer, he obtained this and drank it up. Shortly afterwards he found that his cough was quite cured, and then it occurred to him that he had hit upon a **capital remedy**. When he reached the city, he learned that a great many doctors had already tried their hand upon the patient,

⁵ <note>This story is a biting **satire** on the medical profession in imperial China. At the time, there were no formal medical diplomas or licensing boards. Instead, the medical ranks were often filled by "failed scholars"—men who had spent their lives studying for the **imperial competitive examinations** but, having failed to secure a government post, turned to medicine as a secondary career. ### CXLI.

## SNOW IN SUMMER.

On the 6th day of the 7th lunar month <note>This would be approximately August, typically the hottest time of the year.</note> in the year of the Fire Pig <note>original: *Ting-Hai*, 1647</note>, there was a heavy fall of snow at Suzhou <note>original: *Soochow*</note>. The people were in a great state of alarm at this omen and went to the temple of the local Rain God <note>original Latin: *Jupiter Pluvius*; the text refers to him as the "Great Prince"</note> to pray for relief. 

Then, a spirit possessed one of the worshippers and moved him to say: "You currently address me as *Your Honor*. Address me instead as *Your Excellency*, and even though I am only a minor deity, it may be well worth your while to do so." 

Thereupon, the people began to use the higher title, and the snow stopped at once. From this, I conclude that flattery is just as pleasant to the ears of gods as it is to the ears of men. <note>This is a satirical jab at the superstitious practice of praying for weather, a custom observed in China by everyone from the Emperor <note>original: *Son of Heaven*</note> down to the poorest farmer. Natural disasters like droughts, floods, and unseasonable weather were viewed as expressions of divine anger, supposedly only to be cured by public prayer and repentance.</note>

### CXLII.

## PLANCHETTE <note>A method of spirit-writing or "automatic writing" used to communicate with the spirit world, known in Chinese as *fuji*.</note>

At Changshan <note>original: Ch‘ang-shan</note> there lived a man named Wang Juiting <note>original: Wang Jui-t‘ing</note>, who was skilled in the art of spirit-writing <note>original: planchette</note>. He

---

<margin>
Spirit-writing was extremely popular in China at the time these stories were written, over 200 years ago, and it remains common today. The character *ji* <note>original: *chi*</note>, used here to refer to the practice, is defined in the *Shuo Wen Jiezi* <note>original: *Shuo Wên*; an influential Chinese dictionary published around 100 AD</note> as "to inquire by divination on doubtful topics." However, that ancient dictionary does not describe the specific method used to obtain the answers. 

To better understand this from personal experience, I recently attended a session at a temple in Xiamen <note>original: Amoy</note> and watched the entire performance. After some time, I was asked to write a question on a slip of paper for the God. I took a pencil and wrote: "A humble seeker asks if he will win the Manila lottery" <note>At the time of this translation in the late 19th century, the Spanish-run lottery in Manila was very popular across East Asia.</note>. 

This question was placed on the altar at the feet of the deity. Soon after, two respectable-looking men—who were not priests—approached a small table covered in sand. Each held one arm of a forked wooden tool. At the point where the two arms met, there was a small wooden peg pointing downward at a right angle. 

As assistants burned piles of spirit-money <note>original: joss-paper</note>, the two men began to whirl the wooden tool around rapidly, pressing the vertical point into the sand. Suddenly, the movement stopped, and the point of the tool quickly traced a character in the sand. This character was immediately identified by the onlookers.

## FRIENDSHIP WITH FOXES.

By-and-by, the entertainment being over, the guest took his leave ; and on looking back the beautiful rooms and their contents had all disappeared. ### 144. (CXLIV)

## THE GREAT RAT

During the reign of the Emperor Wan Li <note>The Wanli Emperor (reigned 1572–1620) was the 14th ruler of the Ming Dynasty. His reign is famous for both its cultural achievements, such as the production of "blue and white" porcelain, and the beginning of the dynasty's internal decline.</note>, the palace was troubled by the presence of a huge rat, quite as big as a cat, which ate up all the cats that were set to catch it. 

Just then it chanced that among the tribute <note>Tribute refers to gifts sent by foreign states or provinces to the Emperor to acknowledge his authority.</note> offerings sent by some foreign State was a lion-cat <term>lion-cat: Often identified as a Persian cat or a similar long-haired breed, prized for their exotic appearance and hunting prowess.</term>, as white as snow. This cat was accordingly put into the room where the rat usually appeared; and, the door being closely shut, a secret watch was kept. 

By-and-by the rat came out of its hole and rushed at the cat, which turned and fled, finally jumping up on the table. The rat followed, upon which the cat jumped down; and thus they went on up and down for some time. Those who were watching said the cat was afraid and of no use; however, in a little while the rat began to jump less briskly, and soon after squatted down out of breath. 

Then the cat rushed at it, and, seizing the rat by the back of the neck, shook and shook while its victim squeaked and

### CXLV.

## WOLVES.

I.—A certain village butcher, who had bought some meat at market and was returning home in the evening, suddenly came across a wolf, which followed him closely, its mouth watering at the sight of what he was carrying. The butcher drew his knife and drove the animal off; and then reflecting that his meat was the attraction, he determined to hang it up in a tree and fetch it the next morning. This he accordingly did, and the wolf followed him no further; but when he went at daylight to recover his property, he saw something hanging up in the tree resembling a human corpse. It turned out to be the wolf, which, in its efforts to get at the meat, had been caught on the meat-hook like a fish; and as the skin of a wolf was just then worth ten ounces of silver <note>The "ounce" refers to the tael, a unit of weight for silver currency. Ten taels was a substantial amount of money for a rural laborer in the 17th century.</note>, the butcher found himself possessed of quite a little capital. Here we have a laughable instance of the result of “climbing trees to catch fish.” <note>original: "緣木求魚" (yuan mu qiu yu). This is a famous satirical remark from the philosopher Mencius. It usually refers to a pursuit that is both impossible and ill-advised, like looking for a fish in a treetop. Here, the author uses it ironically because the wolf actually did find "bait" in a tree, leading to its death.</note>

II.—A butcher, while travelling along at night, was sore pressed by a wolf, and took refuge in an old mat

### 146.

## A SINGULAR VERDICT.

A servant in the employ of a Mr. Sun was sleeping alone one night, when all of a sudden he was arrested and carried before the tribunal of the Ruler of Purgatory <note>The Ruler of Purgatory, or Yama (Yanluo Wang), is the king and judge of the underworld in Chinese mythology.</note>. “This is not the right man,” cried His Majesty, and immediately sent him back to the world of the living. However, after this experience, the servant was afraid to sleep in that bed again and moved his quarters elsewhere. But another servant, named Kuo Ngan, seeing the vacant place, went and occupied it. 

A third servant, named Li Lu, who had a long-standing grudge against the first man, stole up to the bed that same night with a knife in his hand and killed Kuo Ngan <note>original footnote 1: This was the man whose destiny it was really to die just then and appear before the Ruler of Purgatory.</note> by mistake, thinking he was his enemy. Kuo’s father at once brought the case before the magistrate <note>In imperial China, a magistrate acted as the local judge, police chief, and administrator.</note> of the place, pleading that the murdered man was his only son upon whom he depended for his living. The magistrate decided that Li Lu was to take the place of the dead son and serve the father—a decision that left the old man quite distressed. Truly, the first servant's descent into Purgatory was not as marvelous as the magistrate’s decision!

<term>Li Lu</term> (Lǐ Lù): The name of the servant who committed the murder.
<term>magistrate</term> (zhìxiàn): The local official responsible for delivering justice.
<term>Purgatory</term> (Dìyù): The underworld or "Earth Prison" where souls are judged.
<term>singular verdict</term>: An unusual or extraordinary legal judgment.

The dog, on seeing what was done, whined piteously, and jumping into the river, seized the bundle with his teeth and did its best to keep the trader above water until at length a shallow spot was reached. ## CXLIX.

### THE ALCHEMIST.¹

AT Ch'ang-ngan <note>Modern-day Xi'an, which served as the capital for many of China’s greatest dynasties and was a hub of culture and learning.</note> there lived a scholar named Chia Tzŭ-lung, who one day noticed a very refined-looking stranger; and, on making inquiries about him, learnt that he was a Mr. Chên, who had taken lodgings hard by. Accordingly, next day Chia called and sent in his card <note>In traditional Chinese society, visiting cards—slips of paper with one’s name and titles—were essential for formal introductions between members of the scholar-official class.</note>, but did not see Chên, who happened to be out at the time. The same thing occurred thrice; and at length Chia engaged some one to watch and let him know when Mr. Chên was at home. However, even then the latter would not come forth to receive his guest, and Chia had to go in and rout him out. The two now entered into conversation, and soon became mutually charmed with each other; and by-and-by Chia sent off a servant to bring wine from a neighbouring wine-shop. Mr. Chên proved himself a pleasant boon companion, and when the wine was nearly finished, he went to a box, and took from it some wine-cups and a large and beautiful jade

## CL.

# RAISING THE DEAD.

Mr. T'ang P'ing, who attained the highest imperial degree <term>Jinshi: The "Presented Scholar" degree, the most prestigious level of the civil service examinations in imperial China.</term> in the year 1661, was suffering from a long and lingering illness. Suddenly, he felt a warm glow rising from his extremities upward. By the time it had reached his knees, his feet were perfectly numb and without sensation; and before long, his knees and the lower part of his body were similarly affected. 

Gradually, this warmth worked its way up until it reached his heart, <note>In traditional Chinese medicine and philosophy, the heart (xin) is the seat of the mind, consciousness, and moral character. Giles refers back to his earlier notes on the duality of the soul.</note> and then some painful moments ensued. Every single incident of Mr. T'ang's life from his boyhood upwards, no matter how trivial, seemed to surge through his mind, borne along on the tide of his heart's blood. At the remembrance of any virtuous act of his, he experienced a delicious feeling of peace and calm; but when any wicked deed passed before his mind, a painful disturbance took place within him, like oil boiling and fretting in a cauldron. He was quite unable to describe the pangs he suffered; however, he mentioned that he could recollect having stolen, when only seven or eight years—

## <term>FENG-SHUI: Literally "wind and water," this refers to the traditional Chinese system of geomancy used to harmonize individuals with their surrounding environment to ensure good fortune.</term>¹

At <term>I-chow: A region in Shandong province, known today as the city of Linyi.</term> there lived a high official named Sung, whose family were all ardent supporters of Fêng-Shui; so much so, that even the women-folk read books² on the subject, and understood the principles of the science. When Mr. Sung died, his two sons set up separate establishments,³ and each invited to his own house <term>geomancers: Specialized practitioners who interpret the landscape and spiritual flows to determine the best locations for graves and buildings.</term> from far and near, who had any reputation

---

<margin>1: Literally, “wind and water,” or that which cannot be seen and that which cannot be grasped. I have explained the term in my *Chinese Sketches*, p. 143, as “a system of geomancy, by the *science* of which it is possible to determine the desirability of sites—whether of tombs, houses, or cities, from the configuration of such natural objects as rivers, trees, and hills, and to foretell with certainty the fortunes of any family, community, or individual, according to the spot selected; by the *art* of which it is in the power of the geomancer to counteract evil influences by good ones, to transform straight and noxious outlines into undulating and propitious curves, and rescue whole districts from the devastations of flood or pestilence.”</margin>

<margin>2: As a rule, only the daughters of wealthy families receive any education to speak of. <note>In the Qing dynasty context, literacy among women was a marker of high social status, though their education usually focused on moral texts rather than technical manuals like those for geomancy.</note></margin>

There was a man in our village who lived a very dishonorable and immoral life. One morning, when he got up quite early, two men appeared and led him away to the market-place. ### CLIV.

## THE SHE-WOLF AND THE HERD-BOYS.

### CLVII.

## THE ROC.

Two herons built their nests under one of the ornaments on the roof of a temple at **Tientsin** <note>Now known as Tianjin, a major port city in Northern China.</note>. The accumulated dust of years in the shrine below concealed a huge serpent, having the diameter of a washing-basin; and whenever the heron’s young were ready to fly, the reptile proceeded to the nest and swallowed every one of them, to the great distress of the bereaved parents. This took place three years consecutively, and people thought the birds would build there no more. 

However, the following year they came again; and when the time was drawing nigh for their young ones to take wing, away they flew, and remained absent for nearly three days. On their return, they went straight to the nest, and began amidst much noisy chattering to feed their young ones as usual. Just then the serpent crawled up to reach his prey; and as he was nearing the nest the parent-birds flew out and screamed loudly in mid-air. Immediately, there was heard a mighty flapping of wings, and darkness came over the face of the earth, which the astonished spectators now perceived to be caused by a huge bird obscuring the light of the sun <note>This creature is the **Dapeng** (大鵬) or "Great Peng," a giant bird from Chinese mythology often compared to the Arabian "Roc." It was famously described by the philosopher Zhuangzi as being so large that its wings were like clouds filling the sky.</note>. Down it swooped **with**

### CLVIII

## THE FAITHFUL GANDER. <note>original: "Yi Yan" (The Heroic Goose). This story serves as a moral parable about the capacity for loyalty and grief in the animal kingdom.</note>

A sportsman of <term>Tientsin<note>Now known as Tianjin, a major port city in Northern China.</note></term>, having snared a wild goose, was followed to his home by the gander, which flew round and round him in great distress, and only went away at nightfall. Next day, when the sportsman went out, there was the bird again; and at length it alighted quite close to his feet. He was on the point of seizing it when suddenly it stretched out its neck and disgorged a piece of pure gold; whereupon, the sportsman, understanding what the bird meant, cried out, “I see! this is to **ransom** your mate, eh?” 

Accordingly, he at once released the goose, and the two birds flew away with many expressions of their mutual joy, leaving to the sportsman nearly three ounces of pure gold. <note>In Chinese tradition, wild geese are celebrated symbols of marital fidelity and "filling the role" of a partner, as they are believed to mate for life and pine for lost mates.</note> Can, then, mere birds have such feelings as these? Of all sorrows there is no sorrow like separation from those we love; and it seems that the same holds good even of dumb animals. <note>The author Pu Songling often ends his stories with these philosophical reflections, challenging the reader to recognize human virtues like loyalty and love in the natural world.</note>

---

<note>Giles refers the reader to Story XXXV, note 3, which discusses other instances in Chinese folklore where animals exhibit human-like morality or provide gold as a reward for kindness.</note>

<summary>A sportsman captures a wild goose, only to have its mate follow him and offer a piece of gold as a ransom. The story concludes with a reflection on the deep emotional capacity and loyalty of animals.</summary>

When His Excellency **Chu** <note>Chu Kuei (1735–1807) was a respected official known for his integrity and service under the Qianlong and Jiaqing Emperors.</note> was **Viceroy** <term>Viceroy<note>The highest-ranking provincial official in Imperial China, overseeing military and civil affairs for one or more provinces.</note></term> of **Kuang-tung** <note>Modern-day Guangdong province in southern China.</note>, there were constant complaints from the traders of mysterious disappearances; sometimes as many as three or four of them disappearing at once and never being seen or heard of again. In Chinese folk religion, this deity acts as a spiritual magistrate who keeps records of the living and the dead and oversees justice in the afterlife.</note></term>, he took to fasting.

### CLXIII.

## ANOTHER SOLOMON.

At T'ai-yüan <note>A historic city and prefecture in Shanxi Province, northern China.</note> there lived a middle-aged woman with her widowed daughter-in-law. The former was on terms of too great intimacy with a notably bad character of the neighbourhood; and the latter, who objected very strongly to this, did her best to keep the man from the house. The elder woman accordingly tried to send the other back to her family, but she would not go; and at length things came to such a pass that the mother-in-law actually went to the **mandarin** <term>mandarin<note>A Western term for a *guan*, or imperial Chinese official, who acted as magistrate, judge, and administrator for a district.</note></term> of the place and charged her daughter-in-law with the offence she herself was committing. When the mandarin inquired the name of the man concerned, she said she had only seen him in the dark and didn't know who he was, referring him for information to the accused. The latter, on being summoned, gave the man's name, but retorted the charge on her mother-in-law; and when the man was confronted with them, he promptly declared both their stories to be false. The mandarin, however, said there was a **case at first sight** <note>original: *primâ facie*. A legal term meaning that on the surface, there is enough evidence to support the claim.</note> against him, and ordered him to

### CLXIV.

## THE INCORRUPT OFFICIAL.

Mr. Wu, the <term>Sub-prefect</term> <note>A mid-ranking administrative official in the Chinese imperial system, specifically serving in Jinan.</note> of Chi-nan <note>The capital city of Shandong Province, known today as Jinan.</note>, was an upright man. He would take no part in the bribery and corruption that were then widespread—practices which the higher authorities not only overlooked but actively profited from. The Prefect <note>The primary administrative head of a prefecture, and Mr. Wu's direct superior.</note> attempted to bully him into joining their corrupt schemes, even resorting to violent insults. At this, Mr. Wu’s temper flared, and he exclaimed, “Though I am only a subordinate official, if you have a grievance against me, you should impeach me through the proper legal channels; you do not have the right to abuse me in this way. I may die, but I will never consent to degrade my office and subvert the course of justice for the sake of **filthy lucre** <note>A traditional term for money or profit that is gained in a dishonorable or shameful way.</note>.”

Seeing this outburst, the Prefect changed his tone and tried to soothe him . . . . [*How dare people claim the current age is corrupt, when it is they themselves who refuse to walk the straight path?*] <note>This bracketed sentence is an authorial commentary by Pu Songling, reflecting on the individual's responsibility for the morality of their era.</note> One day after this, a certain <term>fox-medium</term> <margin>Certain classes of soothsayers are believed by the Chinese to be possessed by foxes, which animals have the power of looking into the future, etc.</margin> came—

# APPENDIX A.

VISITORS to Chinese temples of the <term>Taoist</term> <note>One of the three great religions of China, focusing on living in harmony with the 'Tao' (the Way) and featuring a large pantheon of gods and spirits.</note> persuasion usually make at once for what is popularly known amongst foreigners as the “Chamber of Horrors.” These belong specially to Taoism, or the ethics of Right in the abstract, as opposed to abstract Wrong, and are not found in temples consecrated to the religion of <term>Buddha</term> <note>Buddhism, which originated in India, focuses more on the cycle of rebirth and enlightenment, though in China it merged significantly with Taoist ideas of hell.</note>. Modern Taoism, however, once a purely metaphysical system, is now so leavened with the superstitions of Buddhism, and has borrowed so much material from its younger rival, that an ordinary Chinaman can hardly tell one from the other, and generally regards them as to all intents and purposes the same. 

These rightly-named Chambers of Horrors—for Madame Tussaud <note>A reference to the famous London wax museum which, in the 19th century, was well-known for its 'Chamber of Horrors' featuring criminals and execution scenes.</note> has nothing more ghastly to show in the whole of her wonderful collection—represent the **Ten Courts of Purgatory**, through some or all of which erring souls must pass before they are suffered to be born again into the world under another form, or transferred to the eternal bliss reserved for the righteous alone. 

As a description of these Ten Courts may not be uninteresting to some of my readers, and as the subject has a direct bearing upon many of the stories in the previous collection, I hereto append my translation of a well-known Taoist work¹ <note>original: "Yü Li" (玉曆), which translates to "The Jade Calendar" or "The Divine Panorama." It is a popular religious tract intended to scare readers into moral behavior by detailing the tortures of the afterlife.</note> which is circulated gratuitously all over the Chinese Empire by people who are anxious to lay up a store of good works against the day of reckoning to come. Those who are acquainted with <term>Dante’s Divine Comedy</term> <note>The famous 14th-century Italian poem describing the author's journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise.</note> will recollect that the poet’s idea of a Christian Purgatory was a series of nine lessening circles arranged one above the other, so as to form a cone. The Taoist believes that his Purgatory consists of **Ten Courts of Justice** situated in different positions at the bottom of a great ocean which lies down in

"My wish is to release all souls, and every moon as this day comes round I would wholly or partially remit the punishment of erring shades, and give them life once more in one of the **Six Paths** <note>The six realms of rebirth: gods, demi-gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-dwellers.</note>. The **Judges of the Ten Courts of Purgatory** then agreed that all who led virtuous lives from their youth upwards shall be escorted at their death to the land of the **Immortals**; that all whose balance of good and evil is exact shall escape the bitterness of the **Three States** <note>The three most painful realms of rebirth: those of animals, hungry ghosts, and the hell-bound.</note>, and be born again among men; that those who have repaid their debts of gratitude and friendship, and fulfilled their destiny, yet have a balance of evil against them, shall pass through the various Courts of Purgatory and then be born again amongst men—rich, poor, old, young, diseased or crippled—to be put a second time upon trial. 

Then, if they behave well they may enter into some happy state; but if badly, they will be dragged by horrid devils through all the Courts, suffering bitterly as they go, and will again be born, to endure in life the uttermost of poverty and wretchedness, and in death the everlasting tortures of hell. ### THE FIRST COURT.

His Infernal Majesty Ch'in Kuang is specially in charge of the register of life and death both for old and young, and presides at the judgment-seat in the lower regions. His court is situated in the great Ocean, away beyond the **Wu-chiao rock**, <note>This rock is traditionally considered the gateway or entrance to the Infernal Regions.</note> far to the west near the murky road which leads to the **Yellow Springs**. <term>Yellow Springs: (Huangquan) A traditional Chinese name for the underworld or the realm of the dead.</term> 

Every man and woman dying in old age whose fate it is to be born again into the world—if their record of good and evil works is equally balanced—are sent to the First Court, and from there transferred back to Life. Depending on their past deserts, males may become females, females may become males, the rich may become poor, and the poor may become rich. 

But those whose good deeds are outnumbered by their bad are sent to a terrace on the right of the Court, called the **Terrace of the Mirror of Sin**, which stands ten feet in height. The mirror is about fifty feet <note>literally, "ten armfuls."</note> in circumference and hangs towards the east. Above it are seven characters written horizontally: "Upon the Terrace of the Sin-Mirror, there are no good men." There, the wicked souls are able to see the naughtiness of their own hearts...

Every Buddhist or Taoist priest who receives money for prayers and liturgies, but skips over words and misses out sentences, on arriving at this, the First Court, will be sent to the section for the Completion of Prayer, and there in a small dark room he shall pick out such passages as he has omitted, and make good the deficiency as best he can, by the uncertain light of an infinitesimal wick burning in a gallon of oil. <note>This punishment ironically forces the negligent priest to perform the very mindfulness they lacked in life under nearly impossible conditions.</note> Even good and virtuous priests must also repair any omissions they may have (accidentally) made, and so must every man or woman who in private devotion may have omitted or wrongly repeated any part of the sacred writings from over-earnestness, their attention not being properly fixed on the actual words they repeat. The same applies to female priests. A dispensation from Buddha to remit such punishment is put in force on the first day of each month when the names are entered in the register of the virtuous.

O ye dwellers upon earth, on the 1st day of the 2nd moon <note>This refers to the first day of the second month of the Chinese lunar calendar.</note>, fasting turn to the north and make oath to abstain from evil and fix your thoughts on good, that ye may escape hell! The precepts of Buddha are circulated over the whole world to warn mankind to believe and repent, that when the last hour comes their spirits may be escorted by dark-robed boys to realms of bliss and happiness in the west. <note>The "West" refers to the Western Pure Land (Sukhavati), the paradise of Amitabha Buddha.</note>

This refers to a common historical practice in China where criminals would seek sanctuary in Buddhist or Taoist monasteries to avoid the secular law.</note> those who filch letters, pictures, books, etc. entrusted to their care, and then pretend to have lost them; those who injure a fellow-creature’s ear, eye, hand, foot, fingers, or toes; those who practise as doctors without any knowledge of the medical art; those who will not ransom grown-up slave-girls; <note>It was considered a moral obligation for masters to allow domestic slave-girls to be ransomed for marriage upon reaching maturity (age 15 or 16), rather than keeping them in perpetual service.</note> those who, contracting marriage for the sake of gain, falsely state their ages; or those who in cases of betrothal, before actual marriage, find out that one of the contracting parties is a bad character, and yet do not come forward to say so, but inflict an irreparable wrong on the innocent one;—such offenders, when their quota of crime has been cast up, their youth or age and the consequences of their acts taken into consideration, will be seized by horrid red-faced devils and thrust into the great Hell, and thence despatched to the particular ward in which they are to be tormented. # APPENDIX.

O you men and women of the world, take this book and warn all sinners, or copy it out and circulate it for general information! If you see people sick and ill, give medicine to heal them. If you see people poor and hungry, feed them. If you see people in difficulties, give money to save them. Repent your past errors, and you will be allowed to cancel that evil by future good, so that when the hour arrives you will pass at once into the Tenth Hall <note>The Tenth Hall is the final stage of the underworld, presided over by the King who Turns the Wheel; here, souls are processed for reincarnation back into the world of the living.</note>, and from there return again to existence on earth.

Let those who love all creatures endowed with life, and do not recklessly cut and slay, but teach their children not to harm small animals and insects—let these, on the 1st of the 3rd moon <note>This refers to the first day of the third month of the Chinese lunar calendar, a significant date for making religious vows.</note>, register an oath not to take life, but to aid in preserving it. Thus they will avoid passing through Purgatory <note>The translator uses the Western term "Purgatory" to describe the various courts of the Chinese underworld where souls are cleansed of sin through punishment.</note>, and will also enter at once the Tenth Hall, to be born again in some happy state.

# THE THIRD COURT.

His Infernal Majesty Sung Ti <note>original: "Songdi Wang." The King of the Third Court, who traditionally judges those who were ungrateful or rebellious toward their superiors.</note> reigns at the bottom of the great Ocean, away to the south-east, below the Wu-chiao rock <note>A legendary stone or cliff in the Buddhist underworld.</note>, in the Gehenna of Black Ropes <note>original: "Heisheng." One of the eight great "hot hells" of Buddhist tradition, where sinners are marked with black lines and then cut or sawed along those lines.</note>. This Hall is many leagues wide, and is subdivided into sixteen wards, as follows:—

In the first everything is Salt; above, below, and all round, the eye rests upon Salt alone. The shades <note>A term for the spirits or ghosts of the deceased.</note> feed upon it, and suffer horrid torments in consequence. When the fit has passed away they return to it once again, and suffer agonies more unutterable than before. In the second, the erring shades are bound with cords and carry heavily-weighted cangues <term>cangue: a heavy wooden board or collar worn around the neck as a punishment to shame and restrict the movement of a prisoner</term>. In the third, they are perpetually pierced through the ribs. In the fourth, their faces are scraped with iron and copper knives. In the fifth, their fat is scraped away from their bodies. In the sixth, their hearts and livers are squeezed with pincers. In the seventh, their eyes are gouged. In the eighth, they are flayed <note>Having the skin stripped off the body.</note>. In the ninth, their feet are cut off. In the tenth, their finger-nails and toe-nails are pulled out. In the eleventh their blood is sucked. In the twelfth, they are hung up head downwards. In the thirteenth, their shoulder-bones are split. In the fourteenth, they are tormented by insects and reptiles. In the fifteenth, they are beaten on the thighs. In the sixteenth, their hearts are scratched.

### THE FOURTH COURT.

The **Lord of the Five Senses** <term>Lord of the Five Senses: Known as Wu-guan Wang, this ruler judges sins committed through the physical senses, particularly those involving greed and dishonesty.</term> reigns at the bottom of the great Ocean, far to the east below the **Wu-chiao rock**. <note>original: "Wu-chiao" (五礁), meaning the Rock of the Five Reefs.</note> His Court is many leagues wide and is subdivided into sixteen wards, as follows:

In the sixth, their shoulders are pricked with a trident and the skin rubbed with a hard brush. In the seventh, holes are bored into their flesh. In the eighth, they are made to sit on spikes. In the ninth, they wear iron clothes. In the tenth, they are placed under heavy pieces of wood, stone, earth, or tiles. In the eleventh, their eyes are put out. In the twelfth, their mouths are choked with dust. In the thirteenth, they are perpetually dosed with nasty medicines. In the fourteenth, the ground is so slippery they are always falling down. In the fifteenth, their mouths are painfully pricked. In the sixteenth, their bodies are buried under broken stones, etc., with the head alone being left out.

## THE SIXTH COURT

This Court is situated at the bottom of the great Ocean, due north of the <term>Wu-chiao rock (the "Dark Reef" or "Black Rock" of the Buddhist underworld)</term>. It is a vast, noisy <term>Gehenna (a place of suffering or hell)</term>, many leagues in extent, and around it are sixteen wards.

In the first, the souls are made to kneel for long periods on iron shot. In the second, they are placed up to their necks in filth. In the third, they are pounded till the blood runs out. In the fourth, their mouths are opened with iron pincers and filled full of needles. In the fifth, they are bitten by rats. In the sixth, they are enclosed in a net of thorns and nipped by locusts. In the seventh, they are crushed to a jelly. In the eighth, their skin is lacerated and they are beaten on the raw. In the ninth, their mouths are filled with fire. In the tenth, they are licked by flames. In the eleventh, they are subjected to noisome smells. In the twelfth, they are butted by oxen and trampled on by horses. In the thirteenth, their hearts are scratched. In the fourteenth, their heads are rubbed till their skulls come off. In the fifteenth, they are chopped in two at the waist. In the sixteenth, their skin is taken off and rolled up into spills <note>Thin strips of wood or twisted paper used for lighting fires or lamps.</note>.

# THE EIGHTH COURT.

His Infernal Majesty, King Tu Shi <note>original: "Tu Shih"</note>, reigns at the bottom of the great Ocean, due east below the Five-Reef <note>original: "Wu-chiao"</note> rock, in a vast, noisy Court many leagues in extent, subdivided into sixteen wards as follows:

### THE TENTH COURT.

Amongst those <term>shades <note>The spirits or ghosts of the deceased.</note></term>, on their way to be born again in the world of human beings, there are often to be found women who cry out that they have some old and bitter wrong to avenge <note>The original translator notes that in this cultural context, women were often depicted as having more persistent and intense grievances than men, likely due to their lack of legal recourse in life.</note>, and that rather than be born again amongst men they would prefer to enter the ranks of <term>hungry devils <note>original: "餓鬼" (èguǐ). Beings who suffer from eternal, insatiable hunger and thirst as a result of their past greed or the circumstances of their death.</note></term>. On examining them more closely it generally comes out that they are the virtuous victims of some wicked student <note>In this context, a "student" or scholar refers to a member of the literati class who was studying for the civil service examinations, the primary path to power and status.</note>, who may perhaps have an eye to their money, and accordingly dresses himself out to entrap them, or promises marriage when sometimes he has a wife already, or offers to take care of an aged mother or a late husband’s children. Thus the foolish women are beguiled, and put their property in the wicked man’s hands. By-and-by he turns round upon and reviles them, and, <term>losing face <note>Suffering a devastating loss of social standing or dignity in the eyes of the community.</note></term> in the eyes of their relatives and friends, with no one to redress their wrong, they are driven to commit suicide. 

Then, hearing <note>News travels even within the realms of Purgatory.</note> that their seducer is likely to succeed at the examination, they beg and implore to be allowed to go back and <term>compass <note>To plot, bring about, or achieve.</note></term> his death. Now, although what they urge is true enough, yet that man’s destiny may not be worked out, or the transmitted effects of his ancestors’ virtue may not have passed away <note>The text refers to the concept of 'accumulated merit,' where the good deeds of one's parents or grandparents can act as a spiritual shield for a descendant, delaying their punishment.</note>; therefore, as a compromise, these injured shades are allowed to send a spirit to the <term>Examination Hall <note>The site where imperial civil service exams were held; a place of extreme stress where spiritual interference was commonly feared.</note></term> to hinder and confuse him in the preparation of his paper, or to change the names on the published list of successful candidates; and finally, when his hour arrives, to proceed with the spirit who carries the death-summons, seize him, and bring him to the First Court of judgment.

The place where the <term>Wheel of Fate <note>The cycle of reincarnation, known in Buddhism as Samsara, where souls are assigned to new lives based on their past deeds.</note></term> goes round is many leagues in extent, enclosed on all sides by an iron palisade. Within are eighty-one subdivisions, each of which has its proper officers and magisterial appointments. Beyond the palisade there is a labyrinth of 108,000 paths leading by direct and circuitous routes back to earth. Inside it is as dark as pitch, and through it pass the spirits of priest and layman alike. But to one who looks from the outside everything is seen as clear as crystal, and the attendants who guard the place all have the faces and features they had at their birth. These attendants are chosen from virtuous people who in life were noted for <term>filial piety <note>The Confucian virtue of respect for one's parents, elders, and ancestors, considered the hierarchy upon which society is built.</note></term>, friendship, or respect for life, and are sent here to look after the working of the Wheel and such duties. If for a space of five years they make no mistakes they are promoted to a higher office; but if found to be lazy or careless they are reported to the Throne for punishment.

Those who in life have been unfilial or have destroyed much life, when they have been tortured in the various Courts are brought here and beaten to death with peach twigs <note>In Chinese folklore, peach wood is believed to possess spiritual power capable of subduing demons and punishing spirits.</note>. They then become <term>chien <note>A term referring to a spirit or soul that has been degraded; here it signifies the transition from a human soul to that of a lower animal.</note></term>, and with changed heads and altered faces are turned out into the labyrinth to proceed by the path which ends in the brute creation.

Birds, beasts, fishes and insects, may after many myriads of <term>aeons <note>original: "kalpas." In Buddhist and Hindu cosmology, a kalpa is an immense period of time, often described as the duration of a universe from its creation to its destruction.</note></term> again resume their original shapes; and if there are any that during three existences do not destroy life, they may be born amongst human beings as a reward, a record being made and their names forwarded to the First Court for approval. But all <term>shades <note>The spirits of the deceased.</note></term> of men and women must proceed to the <term>Terrace of Oblivion <note>The pavilion where souls are made to forget their past lives before rebirth.</note></term>.

<term>Mother Mêng <note>Known as Mêng Pó (Grandmother Mêng), she is the goddess of forgetfulness who serves a special brew to souls so they do not remember their previous lives or the trials of the underworld.</note></term> was born in the Earlier Han Dynasty <note>206 BCE – 9 CE.</note>. In her childhood she studied books of the Confucian school; when she grew up she chanted the liturgies of Buddha. Of the past and the future she had no care, but occupied herself in exhorting mankind to desist from taking life and become vegetarians. At eighty-one years of age her hair was white and her complexion like a child's. She lived and died a virgin, calling herself simply Mêng; but men called her Mother Mêng. She retired to the hills and lived as a **nun** <note>original: "religieuse"</note> until the Later Han <note>25 – 220 CE.</note>. Thus they forgot everything that has previously happened to them, and carry away with them to earth some slight weaknesses such as the mouth watering at the thought (of something nice), laughter inducing perspiration, fear inducing tears, anger inducing sobs, or spitting from nervousness. Good spirits who go back into the world will have their senses of sight, hearing, smell, and taste very much increased in power, and their physical strength and constitution generally will be bettered. But evil spirits will experience the exact contrary of this, as a reward for previous sins and as a warning to others to pray and repent.

The Terrace is situated in front of the Ten Courts, outside the six bridges. It is square, measuring ten Chinese feet <note>Approximately 3.3 meters or 11 feet.</note> every way, and surrounded by 108 small rooms. To the east there is a raised path, one foot four inches in breadth, and in the rooms above-mentioned are prepared cups of forgetfulness ready for the arrival of the shades. Whether they swallow much or little it matters not ; but sometimes there are perverse devils who altogether refuse to drink. Then beneath their feet sharp blades start up, and a copper tube is forced down their throats, by which means they are compelled to swallow some. When they have drunk, they are raised by the attendants and escorted back by the same path. They are next pushed on to the <term>Bitter Bamboo floating bridge <note>A symbolic and treacherous crossing that souls must navigate to reach their new life.</note></term>, with torrents of rushing red water on either side. Half way across they perceive written in large characters on a red cliff on the opposite side the following lines :—

> “ To be a man is easy, but to act up to one’s responsibilities as such is hard.
> Yet to be a man once again is harder still.
>
> For those who would be born again in some happy state there is no great 
> difficulty ;
> It is only necessary to keep mouth and heart in harmony.”

They take no thought as to the end that must overtake them; and finally, they bring themselves once more to the same horrid plight.

### ANCESTRAL WORSHIP.

> “The rudimentary form of all religion is the propitiation <note>The act of appeasing or winning the favor of a spirit or deity through gifts or rituals.</note> of dead ancestors, who are supposed to be still existing, and to be capable of working good or evil to their descendants.”—**SPENCER’S ESSAYS** <note>Herbert Spencer (1820–1903) was an English philosopher and sociologist who attempted to apply the theory of evolution to human society and religion.</note>. Vol. iii., p. 102.—*The Origin of Animal Worship*.

### BILOCATION.

> “As a general rule, people are apt to consider it impossible for a man to be in two places at once, and indeed a saying to that effect has become a popular saw.  But the rule is so far from being universally accepted, that the word ‘bilocation’ <term>bilocation <note>The perceived ability of a person to be present in two distinct locations at the exact same time, often associated with saints or supernatural beings.</note></term> has been invented to express the miraculous faculty possessed by certain saints of the Roman Church, of being in two places at once ; like St. Alfonso di Liguori <note>Saint Alphonsus Liguori (1696–1787) was an Italian bishop. Legend says he was seen at the deathbed of Pope Clement XIV in Rome while he was actually in a trance miles away in his own home.</note>, who had the useful power of preaching his sermon in church while he was confessing penitents at home.”—**TYLOR’S** *Primitive Culture* <note>Sir Edward Burnett Tylor (1832–1917) is known as the father of cultural anthropology. This work explored his theories on "animism"—the belief that all things have spirits.</note>.  Vol. i., p. 447.

Vol. iii., p. 104.—*The Origin of Animal Worship*.

### SHADE OR SHADOW.

> “The ghost or phantasm seen by the dreamer or the visionary is an unsubstantial form, like a shadow, and thus the familiar term of the *shade* <note>In English, "shade" is an archaic or literary term for a ghost, derived from the literal shadow cast by an object.</note> comes in to express the soul. Thus the Tasmanian word for the shadow is also that for the spirit; the Algonquin Indians describe a man’s soul as *otahchuk*, ‘his shadow;’ the Quiché language uses *natub* for ‘shadow, soul;’ the Arawac *ueja* means ‘shadow, soul, image;’ the Abipones made the one word *loákal* serve for ‘shadow, soul, echo, image.’”—**TYLOR’S** *Primitive Culture* <note>Sir Edward Burnett Tylor (1832–1917) was a founding figure in cultural anthropology. In this work, he explores "animism"—the belief that all objects, places, and creatures possess a distinct spiritual essence.</note>. Vol. i., p. 430.

### TRANSMIGRATION.

> “As for believers, savage or civilised, in the great doctrine of metempsychosis <term>metempsychosis: a Greek term for the soul moving from one body to another at death, often used interchangeably with reincarnation.</term>, these not only consider that an animal may have a soul, but that this soul may have inhabited a human being, and thus the creature may be in fact their own ancestor or once familiar friend.”—**TYLOR’S** *Primitive Culture*. Vol. i., p. 469.

### TREE-SOULS.

> “Orthodox Buddhism decided against the tree-souls, and consequently against the scruple to harm them, declaring trees to have no mind nor sentient principle, though admitting that certain dewas <term>dewas: derived from the Sanskrit 'deva,' referring to divine beings, spirits, or celestial entities.</term> or spirits do reside in the body of trees, and speak from within them.”—**TYLOR’S** *Primitive Culture*. Vol. i., p. 475.
